lessons.title: Parts of a Cell
lessons.notes_html:
The Cell

All living things are made of tiny units called cells. A cell has a cell membrane, jelly-like cytoplasm and several small structures called organelles, each doing a special job. The cell membrane is composed of proteins and lipids and controls what enters and leaves the cell.

Important Organelles

The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It contains the hereditary material (DNA in chromosomes) and directs all cell activities such as growth, division and production of proteins. The jelly-like material inside the nucleus is called nucleoplasm, while the material between the membrane and the nucleus is the cytoplasm.

Mitochondria produce energy from food, so the site of respiration in a cell is the mitochondria. Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells; they contain the green pigment chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis. A plant cell has one large central vacuole filled with cell sap, which keeps the cell firm; an animal cell has many small vacuoles.

Plant Cell and Animal Cell

A plant cell has a cell wall of cellulose outside the membrane, chloroplasts and one large vacuole. An animal cell has no cell wall and no chloroplasts. The rigid cell wall gives the plant cell a fixed shape, support and protection.

Key Points

  • The nucleus controls the whole cell activity.
  • Mitochondria release energy from food during respiration.
  • Chlorophyll is the green pigment present in chloroplasts.
  • Plant cells have a cell wall; animal cells do not.

mcqs.why: An animal cell contains many small vacuoles, while a plant cell has one large central vacuole filled with cell sap.

mcqs.q: Mitochondria play an important role in:
mcqs.why: Mitochondria release energy from food during respiration, which is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

mcqs.q: Chromosomes are present in:
mcqs.why: Chromosomes, which carry the hereditary material DNA, are present inside the nucleus of the cell.

mcqs.q: The cell membrane is composed of:
mcqs.why: The cell membrane is a thin layer made of proteins and lipids; cellulose is found in the cell wall of plant cells, not in the membrane.

mcqs.q: Chlorophyll is ________ in colour.
mcqs.why: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that traps sunlight for photosynthesis, and it gives leaves their green colour.

mcqs.q: In a cell, the site for respiration is:
mcqs.why: Respiration, which releases energy from food, takes place in the mitochondria of the cell.

mcqs.q: Which organelle controls the whole activity of the cell?
mcqs.why: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell because it contains DNA and directs growth, division and protein production.

mcqs.q: The jelly-like substance between the cell membrane and the nucleus is called:
mcqs.why: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance filling the cell outside the nucleus; nucleoplasm is the jelly inside the nucleus only.

mcqs.q: The large central vacuole of a plant cell is filled with:
mcqs.why: The plant vacuole is filled with cell sap, which presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm (turgid).

mcqs.q: The cell wall of a plant cell is made of:
mcqs.why: The plant cell wall is a strong, rigid layer made of cellulose, present outside the cell membrane, giving shape and protection.

lessons.title: Tissues in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Tissue?

A group of cells of the same kind working together is called a tissue. In plants, epidermal tissue forms the outer protective layer of leaves, stems and roots. Its tiny pores, the stomata, allow exchange of gases. The inner tissue of the leaf, full of chloroplasts, is the mesophyll tissue, where photosynthesis takes place.

Xylem and Phloem

Xylem and phloem together form the vascular (conducting) system of plants. Xylem is made of long, hollow, dead tube-like cells joined end to end; it conducts water and minerals from the roots to the leaves. Phloem is made of living sieve tubes with perforated end walls (sieve plates); it transports prepared food from the leaves to all parts of the plant, upward and downward.

Root System and Shoot System

The part of the plant below the ground is the root system; it absorbs water and minerals and anchors the plant. The part above the ground — stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits — is the shoot system.

Key Points

  • Xylem carries water and minerals upward from roots to leaves.
  • Phloem carries prepared food from leaves to the whole plant.
  • Epidermal tissue protects the plant; stomata exchange gases.
  • Mesophyll tissue of the leaf makes food by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: In plants, water is conducted from roots to leaves by:
mcqs.why: Xylem vessels are hollow tubes that conduct water and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves and other parts.

mcqs.q: Prepared food is transported from the leaves to other parts of the plant by:
mcqs.why: Phloem sieve tubes carry the food prepared in the leaves to all growing and storage parts, in both directions.

mcqs.q: The outer protective layer of leaves and stems is formed by:
mcqs.why: Epidermal tissue is a single layer of flat cells forming the outer skin of the plant, protecting it from water loss and injury.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis in a leaf takes place mainly in the:
mcqs.why: Mesophyll tissue is the inner tissue of the leaf, packed with chloroplasts, and its function is to make food by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which of the following belongs to the root system?
mcqs.why: The root system is the below-ground part of the plant — the roots that absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant.

mcqs.q: Sieve tubes with perforated end walls are part of the:
mcqs.why: Phloem consists of living sieve tubes whose perforated end walls (sieve plates) let prepared food pass from cell to cell.

mcqs.q: The tiny pores in the epidermis of a leaf that allow exchange of gases are called:
mcqs.why: Stomata are tiny pores in the epidermal tissue of leaves through which gases are exchanged and water vapour escapes.

mcqs.q: Xylem vessels are suited to carry water because they are:
mcqs.why: Xylem is made of long, hollow, dead cells joined end to end like pipes, so water rises easily through them from roots to leaves.

mcqs.q: Xylem and phloem together form the ________ system of plants.
mcqs.why: Xylem and phloem are the two conducting tissues, so together they are called the vascular or conducting system of the plant.

mcqs.q: Which part of the plant takes part in making food and reproduction?
mcqs.why: The shoot system — stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits — stands above the ground, makes food and takes part in reproduction.

lessons.title: Tissues, Organs and Systems in Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Animal Tissues

Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body (skin) and the lining of internal organs. Muscle tissue can contract and relax to produce movement; the heart is made of cardiac muscle, which pumps blood without stopping, and the stomach wall has smooth muscle that churns food. Nerve cells (neurons) are long and thin with thread-like fibres, so they carry messages quickly over long distances. Bones are made of hard connective tissue, which gives shape and support and protects soft organs.

Blood — a Connective Tissue

Blood transports substances all over the body. Red blood cells contain the red pigment haemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to all body cells. Blood also carries digested food and hormones, removes wastes, fights germs and clots wounds. The organs of the circulatory system are the heart, arteries (carrying blood away from the heart), veins (bringing blood back) and capillaries.

Organs and Systems

Different organs work together in systems. The kidneys, for example, belong to the excretory system and remove waste from the blood.

Key Points

  • Human skin is made of epithelial tissue.
  • Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back.
  • Muscles move the body; bones support and protect it.

mcqs.q: Human skin is made of:
mcqs.why: The skin is the outer covering of the animal body and is made of epithelial tissue, which also lines the internal organs.

mcqs.q: Oxygen is carried by:
mcqs.why: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which joins with oxygen in the lungs and releases it where the body cells need it.

mcqs.q: The red pigment present in red blood cells is:
mcqs.why: Haemoglobin is the red pigment of red blood cells; it gives blood its red colour and carries oxygen around the body.

mcqs.q: Kidneys perform functions related to the:
mcqs.why: The kidneys filter waste materials from the blood and remove them as urine, so they belong to the excretory system.

mcqs.q: Blood is an example of:
mcqs.why: Blood is a connective tissue that flows through the body, transporting oxygen, food, hormones and wastes between organs.

mcqs.q: The muscle tissue of the heart, which pumps blood throughout life without stopping, is:
mcqs.why: Cardiac muscle tissue contracts and relaxes rhythmically without tiring, pumping blood from the heart to the whole body.

mcqs.q: Nerve cells carry messages quickly because they are:
options: Long and thin with thread-like fibres
mcqs.why: Neurons are long and thin with branched thread-like fibres, like electric wires, so signals travel quickly over long distances.

mcqs.q: Bones are made of hard:
mcqs.why: Bones are made of hard, strong connective tissue; they give shape and support to the body and protect organs like the brain and heart.

mcqs.q: Arteries are the blood vessels that:
options: Bring blood back to the heart
Carry blood away from the heart
mcqs.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to all parts of the body, while veins bring the blood back to the heart.

mcqs.q: The smooth muscle of the stomach wall helps digestion by:
options: Churning food and mixing it with juices
mcqs.why: Smooth muscle in the stomach wall churns the food, mixes it with digestive juices and pushes it onward through the gut.

lessons.title: Sexual Reproduction and the Flower
lessons.notes_html:
The Flower

The flower is the organ of sexual reproduction in a plant. Reproduction needs male and female gametes (reproductive cells): the male gamete is the sperm and the female gamete is the egg.

Male and Female Parts

Sperms are produced inside the pollen grains, which are formed in the anthers of the stamen. The female part of the flower is the carpel (pistil). It has three parts: the stigma, the sticky top that receives pollen; the style, the slender tube-like middle part; and the ovary, the swollen basal part containing the ovules. The egg cell is produced inside the ovule.

How the Gametes Meet

After pollen lands on the stigma, it germinates and grows a pollen tube down through the style to the ovule. The pollen tube carries the sperms to the egg so that they can fuse.

Key Points

  • The flower is the reproductive organ of the plant.
  • Pollen grains are made in the anther; the egg is made in the ovule.
  • The carpel has three parts: stigma, style and ovary.
  • After fertilization, the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovule becomes the seed.

mcqs.q: The organ which takes part in sexual reproduction of a plant is the:
mcqs.why: The flower contains the male and female reproductive parts of the plant, so it is the organ of sexual reproduction.

mcqs.q: The male reproductive cell is called:
mcqs.why: The male gamete is the sperm, produced inside pollen grains; the female gamete is the egg, produced inside the ovule.

mcqs.q: The sticky top part of the carpel that receives pollen grains is the:
mcqs.why: The stigma is the sticky top of the carpel; its stickiness helps it catch and hold the pollen grains landing on it.

mcqs.q: Ovules are present inside the:
mcqs.why: The ovary is the swollen basal part of the carpel and it contains the ovules, each holding an egg cell.

mcqs.q: Pollen grains are produced in the:
mcqs.why: Pollen grains, which contain the male gametes (sperms), are produced in the anthers of the stamens.

mcqs.q: The structure which carries sperms to the ovary is the:
mcqs.why: After landing on the stigma, a pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style, and this tube carries the sperms to the ovule.

mcqs.q: The slender, tube-like middle part of the carpel is the:
mcqs.why: The style is the slender middle part of the carpel through which the pollen tube grows on its way to the ovule.

mcqs.q: After fertilization, the ovary of the flower develops into the:
mcqs.why: After fertilization the ovary wall develops into the fruit, while each fertilized ovule inside becomes a seed.

mcqs.q: The egg cell of a flowering plant is produced inside the:
mcqs.why: The female gamete (egg) is produced inside the ovule, which lies protected within the ovary of the carpel.

mcqs.q: The fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete is called:
mcqs.why: Fertilization is the fusion of a sperm with an egg cell; it forms a zygote, which then grows into the embryo of a new plant.

lessons.title: Pollination and Fertilization
lessons.notes_html:
Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. In self-pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant, as in pea, wheat and tomato. In cross pollination, pollen is carried to a flower of a different plant of the same kind, usually by wind, water or insects, as in maize, papaya and sunflower.

Fertilization

After pollination, the pollen tube delivers two sperms to the ovule. One sperm fuses with the egg to form the zygote, which develops into the embryo. The second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the endosperm, the food store of the seed. Because two fusions take place, this is called double fertilization.

Why So Many Pollen Grains?

A flower produces millions of pollen grains because most are wasted during transfer — blown away, eaten by insects or missing the stigma. Producing a huge number raises the chance that some pollen reaches the ovules. Ovules stay protected inside the ovary, so fewer are needed.

Key Points

  • Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
  • The zygote is formed by fertilization and grows into the embryo.
  • Fusion of a sperm with two polar nuclei forms the endosperm.
  • Self-pollination: same plant. Cross pollination: different plant.

mcqs.q: Pollination is the transfer of:
mcqs.why: Pollination means carrying pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma, by wind, water or insects.

mcqs.q: A zygote is formed as a result of:
mcqs.why: When a sperm fuses with an egg cell (fertilization), the single cell formed is called the zygote.

mcqs.q: A zygote develops into:
mcqs.why: The zygote divides and grows into the embryo, the young plant inside the seed, which later germinates.

mcqs.q: Fusion of a sperm with two polar nuclei forms:
mcqs.why: In double fertilization, one sperm forms the zygote with the egg, and the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the endosperm (food store).

mcqs.q: Self-pollination commonly occurs in:
mcqs.why: In pea (also wheat and tomato), anthers and stigma of the same flower mature together, so pollen easily reaches the same flower's stigma.

mcqs.q: Cross pollination commonly occurs in:
mcqs.why: In maize, pollen is carried by wind from one plant to the flowers of other plants, which is cross pollination.

mcqs.q: In self-pollination, pollen is transferred to the stigma of:
options: The same flower or same plant
mcqs.why: Self-pollination means the pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower, or of another flower on the same plant.

mcqs.q: Cross pollination is usually carried out by:
mcqs.why: Pollen cannot move by itself between plants; wind, water and insects act as agents that carry it in cross pollination.

mcqs.q: The endosperm in a seed works as the:
mcqs.why: The endosperm, formed by fusion of a sperm with two polar nuclei, stores food that nourishes the growing embryo.

mcqs.q: A flower produces millions of pollen grains because:
options: Most pollen is wasted during transfer
mcqs.why: Most pollen is blown away, eaten or misses the stigma, so a huge number is produced to make sure some pollen reaches the ovules.

lessons.title: Asexual Reproduction in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Vegetative Propagation

In asexual reproduction only one parent takes part, without gametes or fertilization, and the new plants are exact copies of the parent. Natural methods include runners (thin stems running along the ground, as in strawberry and doob grass), tubers (potato), bulbs (onion, garlic) and rhizomes (ginger, turmeric) — underground stems that store food and bear buds.

Artificial Methods

In cutting, a stem piece with buds is planted in moist soil (rose, sugarcane). In layering, a branch is bent and buried in soil while still attached to the parent until it roots (jasmine). In grafting, a stem piece called the scion is joined onto the rooted stock of another plant (mango, apple). In budding, only a single bud is inserted into the stock (roses, citrus).

Advantages

New plants keep the parent's good qualities exactly, grow and bear fruit faster than seed-grown plants, and even seedless plants like banana can be multiplied.

Key Points

  • Asexual reproduction has one parent and no fertilization.
  • Scion = upper desired piece; stock = lower rooted part.
  • Budding uses one bud; grafting uses a whole stem piece.
  • Vegetative plants are exact copies of the parent.

mcqs.q: Asexual reproduction in which the stem is buried in the soil near the parent plant is called:
mcqs.why: In layering, a branch still attached to the parent is bent down and buried in soil; it roots there and is then cut off as a new plant.

mcqs.q: An example of natural vegetative propagation is:
options: Runners growing into a new plant
mcqs.why: Runners are natural: the stem runs along the ground and grows roots and a new shoot at its nodes, as in strawberry and doob grass.

mcqs.q: Production of a new plant from an underground stem is an example of:
mcqs.why: Underground stems like tubers, bulbs and rhizomes grow new plants from buds without gametes, so this is asexual reproduction.

mcqs.q: A potato plant is propagated by its:
mcqs.why: The potato is a tuber — a swollen underground stem storing food, whose buds (eyes) grow into new potato plants.

mcqs.q: In grafting, the rooted lower part of the plant is called the:
mcqs.why: The stock is the lower, rooted part that absorbs water and minerals; the scion is fixed on it and gives the desired variety.

mcqs.q: In grafting, the stem piece taken from the plant whose fruit quality is desired is the:
mcqs.why: The scion is the upper piece, taken from a plant of desired quality, which grows on the stock and produces that quality of fruit.

mcqs.q: Budding differs from grafting because in budding:
options: A whole stem piece is used
Only a single bud is used
mcqs.why: In budding, only one bud of the desired plant is inserted under the bark of the stock; grafting joins a whole stem piece (scion).

mcqs.q: Rose and sugarcane are commonly propagated by:
mcqs.why: A stem cutting with buds is planted in moist soil; it grows roots below and a shoot above, forming a new plant like the parent.

mcqs.q: Plants produced by asexual reproduction are:
mcqs.why: Only one parent takes part and no gametes fuse, so the offspring have exactly the same qualities as the parent plant.

mcqs.q: Plants like banana and seedless grapes, which do not produce useful seeds, are multiplied by:
mcqs.why: Since such plants cannot be grown from seeds, farmers multiply them vegetatively by cuttings, suckers or other plant parts.

lessons.title: Energy-Giving and Body-Building Foods
lessons.notes_html:
Why Do We Need Food?

We need food because it provides energy for all activities, materials for growth and repair of the body, and protection against diseases. Food supplies the nutrients our body needs every day.

Carbohydrates — Energy-Giving Foods

Carbohydrates are the main and immediate source of energy. Their sources are rice, wheat, maize, potato, bread, sugar, honey and fruits like banana and mango. Starch is a carbohydrate found in foods like potato. Sugars give quick energy, while starchy foods give lasting energy.

Proteins — Body-Building Foods

Proteins are called the building blocks of the body. They build new cells and tissues, repair worn-out parts and help children grow. Sources are meat, fish, egg, milk, cheese, pulses (dal), beans, soyabean and nuts.

Fats — Stored Energy

Fats give concentrated energy — more than double the energy of carbohydrates. They keep the body warm and protect delicate organs. Sources are butter, ghee, vegetable oils, cream, cheese and nuts. Vegetable oils belong to the fats group.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates give energy; proteins build the body; fats store energy.
  • Fish, egg, meat and pulses are rich in proteins.
  • Butter and oils are the best sources of fats.
  • Growing children need extra proteins for growth.

mcqs.q: The immediate source of energy is:
mcqs.why: Fruits like mango contain sugars that are absorbed quickly, so they act as an immediate source of energy for the body.

mcqs.q: Food rich in proteins is:
mcqs.why: Fish is a body-building food rich in proteins, while bread, potato and rice are mainly rich in carbohydrates.

mcqs.q: Which food is best for providing fats?
mcqs.why: Butter is almost pure fat, so it is the best source of fats among these foods; fats give concentrated energy and warmth.

mcqs.q: Which food is rich in carbohydrates?
mcqs.why: Starch itself is a carbohydrate; starchy foods like potato, rice and wheat are the rich sources of carbohydrates.

mcqs.q: A good source of starch is:
mcqs.why: Potato stores starch as its food reserve, making it a rich source of this energy-giving carbohydrate.

mcqs.q: Vegetable oils belong to the food group of:
mcqs.why: Vegetable oils are liquid fats obtained from seeds and nuts, so they belong to the fats group of foods.

mcqs.q: Proteins are called the ________ of our body.
mcqs.why: Proteins build new cells and tissues and repair worn-out parts, so they are called the building blocks of the body.

mcqs.q: The main function of carbohydrates in the body is to:
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are the body's main fuel; they are broken down to release energy for all activities, from walking to thinking.

mcqs.q: Which of these foods is rich in proteins?
mcqs.why: Pulses such as dal, beans and chickpeas are rich plant sources of proteins, the body-building nutrient.

mcqs.q: Extra carbohydrates eaten by the body are:
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates eaten in excess of the body's needs are stored in the body and used later when energy is required.

lessons.title: Vitamins and Minerals
lessons.notes_html:
Vitamins — Protective Foods

Vitamins are needed in small amounts but are essential for health. Vitamin A (from carrot, mango, papaya, spinach, milk and egg yolk) keeps eyes and skin healthy; its deficiency causes night blindness. Vitamin C (from citrus fruits like orange, lemon, amla and guava) heals wounds and prevents scurvy. Vitamin D makes bones and teeth strong; it comes from milk, egg yolk, fish, butter and sunlight, in which our skin makes it.

Minerals

Minerals build body parts and control body processes. Iron (from meat, liver, spinach, dates) makes haemoglobin in blood. Calcium (from milk and cheese) builds bones and teeth. Iodine (from iodized salt) helps the thyroid gland; its deficiency causes goitre. Table salt is a mineral — sodium chloride — and provides the mineral sodium.

The Balanced Diet of an Infant

For an infant, milk is the balanced diet, because it contains nearly all the nutrients a baby needs in proper amounts.

Key Points

  • Carrot is a rich source of vitamin A.
  • Vitamin D makes our bones strong.
  • Iron is a mineral, needed to make haemoglobin.
  • Citrus fruits are rich in vitamin C.

mcqs.q: A rich source of vitamin A is:
mcqs.why: Carrots and other yellow-orange fruits and green leafy vegetables are rich in vitamin A, which keeps eyes and skin healthy.

mcqs.q: Which vitamin makes our bones strong?
mcqs.why: Vitamin D helps the body use calcium to build strong bones and teeth; its deficiency in children causes rickets.

mcqs.q: Iron is a:
mcqs.why: Iron is a mineral, not a vitamin; the body uses it to make haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of red blood cells.

mcqs.q: The balanced diet for an infant is:
mcqs.why: Milk contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals in proper amounts for a baby, so it is the infant's balanced diet.

mcqs.q: Citrus fruits like orange and lemon are rich in:
mcqs.why: Citrus fruits are the well-known sources of vitamin C, which prevents scurvy and helps wounds to heal.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of iodine causes:
mcqs.why: Iodine deficiency makes the thyroid gland in the neck swell, a condition called goitre; using iodized salt prevents it.

mcqs.q: The mineral provided by table salt is:
mcqs.why: Table salt is sodium chloride (NaCl), so it provides the mineral sodium, needed for balancing body fluids.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of vitamin A causes:
mcqs.why: Without vitamin A a person cannot see clearly in dim light — this is night blindness; carrots, mango and eggs prevent it.

mcqs.q: Our skin makes vitamin D with the help of:
mcqs.why: When sunlight falls on the skin, the skin makes vitamin D, which is why sunlight is called a natural source of this vitamin.

mcqs.q: Calcium, which builds bones and teeth, is obtained from:
mcqs.why: Milk, cheese and other dairy foods are rich in calcium, the mineral that builds and strengthens bones and teeth.

lessons.title: Balanced Diet and the Food Pyramid
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Balanced Diet?

A balanced diet contains all the essential nutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage — in proper amounts according to the age and work of a person. It gives energy, helps growth and repair, and protects us from diseases by keeping the immune system strong.

Unbalanced Diet

An unbalanced diet is one in which one or more essential nutrients are missing, or present in too much or too little quantity. Eating only one type of food, or too much fat and sugar with too few proteins and vitamins, leads to weakness, poor growth and deficiency diseases.

The Food Pyramid

A food pyramid is a chart shaped like a pyramid that guides us in choosing the right food in the right amount. Cereals, bread and rice are at the wide base (eat most); fruits and vegetables come next; milk, meat and pulses are above them in smaller quantity; and fats, oils and sweets are at the narrow top (eat least).

Why Eat from All Groups?

No single food contains all the nutrients. If any group is missing, the body suffers from deficiency, so we must eat from all food groups in proper amounts.

Key Points

  • A balanced diet has all nutrients in proper amounts.
  • The food pyramid shows what to eat most and what to eat least.
  • Fats, oils and sweets are at the top of the pyramid — eat least.
  • An unbalanced diet causes weakness and deficiency diseases.

mcqs.q: A balanced diet is the food containing:
options: Proper amounts of all essential nutrients
mcqs.why: A balanced diet supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water in the proper amounts the body needs.

mcqs.q: A food pyramid is a chart that helps us in:
options: Choosing the right food in the right amount
mcqs.why: The pyramid-shaped chart guides us to take each food group in the right quantity to plan a balanced diet.

mcqs.q: The foods placed at the wide base of the food pyramid, which we should eat in large quantity, are:
mcqs.why: Cereals, bread and rice form the wide base of the pyramid, showing they should make the largest part of our daily diet.

mcqs.q: Fats, oils and sweets are placed at the narrow top of the food pyramid because they should be eaten:
mcqs.why: The narrow top of the pyramid shows that fats, oils and sweets are needed only in small amounts; excess makes us obese.

mcqs.q: A diet in which one or more essential nutrients are missing is called:
mcqs.why: An unbalanced diet lacks some nutrients or has them in wrong amounts, and it leads to weakness, poor growth and diseases.

mcqs.q: The proper amount of nutrients in a balanced diet depends on a person's:
mcqs.why: A balanced diet is planned according to age and work: a growing child and a hard-working labourer need more energy and protein.

mcqs.q: Besides the nutrients, a balanced diet also includes:
mcqs.why: Water and roughage (fibre) are essential parts of a balanced diet; water carries nutrients and roughage helps the gut work properly.

mcqs.q: Eating only one type of food for a long time leads to:
mcqs.why: No single food has all nutrients, so eating only one type causes deficiency of the missing nutrients and diseases follow.

mcqs.q: A balanced diet protects us from diseases because it:
options: Stops all germs in the air
mcqs.why: Proper nutrients keep the immune system strong, so a person eating a balanced diet falls ill less often and recovers faster.

mcqs.q: We should eat from all food groups because:
options: Each group has a different colour
No single food contains all the nutrients
It is a school rule only
It makes the plate look full
mcqs.why: Every food group supplies different nutrients — energy, building material or protection — so all groups are needed for a balanced diet.

lessons.title: Deficiency Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Deficiency Diseases?

Diseases caused by the lack of a nutrient in the diet are called deficiency diseases. Each nutrient's deficiency produces a particular disorder, and eating the missing nutrient prevents or cures it.

Important Deficiency Disorders

Deficiency of vitamin A causes night blindness. Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy — bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds. Deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets — soft, bending bones in children. Deficiency of iron causes anaemia — shortage of haemoglobin, making a person pale, weak and tired. Deficiency of calcium makes bones and teeth weak.

Protein Deficiency

People who do not eat meat can get proteins from pulses, beans, chickpeas, soyabean, milk, cheese and nuts. Long-term protein deficiency causes stunted growth, weak muscles, swelling of the body (kwashiorkor in children) and weak immunity. The body itself contains many proteins, such as haemoglobin in blood, keratin in hair and nails, and insulin, a hormone.

Key Points

  • Scurvy — vitamin C deficiency; prevented by citrus fruits.
  • Rickets — vitamin D deficiency; prevented by milk and sunlight.
  • Anaemia — iron deficiency; prevented by meat, spinach and dates.
  • Glucose is the body's immediate source of energy.

mcqs.q: To prevent scurvy, we should eat foods rich in:
mcqs.why: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency; citrus fruits, amla, guava and tomatoes supply vitamin C and prevent it.

mcqs.q: Rickets in children is prevented by eating foods rich in:
mcqs.why: Rickets is the softening and bending of bones due to vitamin D deficiency; milk, egg yolk, fish and sunlight prevent it.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of iron causes:
mcqs.why: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; its deficiency causes anaemia, in which a person becomes pale, weak and easily tired.

mcqs.q: Anaemia is the shortage of ________ in the blood.
mcqs.why: In anaemia the blood has too little haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the body cells and the person feels weak.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of calcium causes:
mcqs.why: Calcium builds bones and teeth; without enough calcium, bones become soft and weak and teeth decay quickly.

mcqs.q: Night blindness can be prevented by eating:
mcqs.why: These foods are rich in vitamin A, whose deficiency causes night blindness — the inability to see clearly in dim light.

mcqs.q: The body needs glucose as:
mcqs.why: Glucose is quickly absorbed into the blood and used by cells at once, so the body needs it as an immediate source of energy.

mcqs.q: Long-term deficiency of proteins in children causes:
mcqs.why: Without proteins the body cannot build or repair tissues, so children show stunted growth, weak muscles and swelling (kwashiorkor).

mcqs.q: A person who does not eat meat can meet protein needs from:
mcqs.why: Plant and dairy foods — pulses, beans, chickpeas, soyabean, milk and cheese — supply proteins to people who do not eat meat.

mcqs.q: Bleeding and swollen gums with slow healing of wounds are symptoms of:
mcqs.why: These are the classic symptoms of scurvy, the disease caused by deficiency of vitamin C in the diet.

lessons.title: Digestion and the Alimentary Canal
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Digestion?

Digestion is the breaking down of large, complex and insoluble food molecules into small, simple and soluble molecules, so that they can be absorbed into the blood. Carbohydrates, proteins and fats must be broken down because in their large form they cannot pass through the walls of the intestine.

The Alimentary Canal

The alimentary canal is a long tube, about 9 metres long. Its parts in order are: oral cavity (mouth), pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum and anus. Together with the digestive glands it forms the digestive system.

In the Oral Cavity

The teeth chew and grind food into small pieces; this increases its surface area so enzymes act quickly. The salivary glands secrete saliva, which moistens and softens the food and whose enzyme amylase starts the digestion of starch. The tongue rolls the food into a ball called the bolus.

The Oesophagus

The oesophagus is a muscular tube that pushes the bolus into the stomach by wave-like movements called peristalsis. No digestion takes place in it.

Key Points

  • Digestion changes insoluble food into soluble molecules.
  • Saliva is secreted by the salivary glands in the oral cavity.
  • Amylase in saliva begins the digestion of starch.
  • Peristalsis pushes food through the oesophagus.

mcqs.q: Digestion is the process of breaking down food into:
mcqs.why: Digestion converts large, complex, insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed into the blood.

mcqs.q: Salivary glands secrete:
mcqs.why: The salivary glands in the oral cavity secrete saliva, which moistens food and starts starch digestion with its enzyme amylase.

mcqs.q: Saliva is produced in the:
mcqs.why: Saliva is produced by the salivary glands located in the oral cavity (mouth) and is mixed with food during chewing.

mcqs.q: The enzyme present in saliva that begins the digestion of starch is:
mcqs.why: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) starts changing starch into sugar in the mouth; pepsin and trypsin act on proteins, lipase on fats.

mcqs.q: Chewing is important for digestion because it:
options: Grinds food into small pieces, increasing surface area for enzymes
mcqs.why: Chewing cuts food into small pieces so enzymes can act on a larger surface area quickly, and mixes food with saliva for swallowing.

mcqs.q: The muscular tube from the oral cavity to the stomach is the:
mcqs.why: The oesophagus is the muscular tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach; it transports food by peristalsis.

mcqs.q: The wave-like muscular movements that push food through the oesophagus are called:
mcqs.why: Peristalsis is the wave-like contraction of the gut muscles that pushes the bolus from the oesophagus into the stomach.

mcqs.q: The alimentary canal is about ________ long.
mcqs.why: The alimentary canal, from mouth to anus, is a long tube of about 9 metres in an adult human being.

mcqs.q: The small ball of chewed food formed by the tongue is called:
mcqs.why: After chewing and mixing with saliva, the tongue rolls the food into a small ball called the bolus, ready for swallowing.

mcqs.q: After passing through the pharynx, swallowed food enters the:
mcqs.why: The order of the canal is oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus and then the stomach; the trachea is the windpipe, not part of digestion.

lessons.title: Digestion in the Stomach and Small Intestine
lessons.notes_html:
The Stomach

The stomach is a J-shaped muscular bag. It stores food temporarily and churns it with gastric juice, turning it into a soup-like mixture called chyme. Gastric juice, secreted by the gastric glands in the stomach wall, contains hydrochloric acid, which kills germs in the food, and the enzyme pepsin, which starts the digestion of proteins.

The Small Intestine

Most digestion takes place in the small intestine. Here food is mixed with bile from the liver, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice. Their enzymes complete digestion: carbohydrates are changed into simple sugars (glucose), proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

Liver and Pancreas

The liver is a digestive gland that is not in contact with the food itself. It produces bile, which contains no enzyme but breaks large fat drops into tiny droplets. The pancreas produces pancreatic juice with enzymes for carbohydrates, proteins and fats, poured into the small intestine.

Key Points

  • Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills germs in food.
  • Pepsin starts protein digestion in the stomach.
  • Most digestion is completed in the small intestine.
  • Bile is made by the liver; it acts on fats.

mcqs.q: Germs in the food are killed in the stomach by:
mcqs.why: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which kills germs entering with food and provides the acidic medium for pepsin.

mcqs.q: Most of the digestion takes place in the:
mcqs.why: In the small intestine, bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice complete the digestion of all foods, so most digestion happens there.

mcqs.q: Which part of the digestive system is not in contact with food?
mcqs.why: The liver is a gland whose juice (bile) reaches the food through a duct; food never passes through the liver itself.

mcqs.q: Digestive enzymes convert starch into:
mcqs.why: Amylase enzymes break starch down step by step into simple sugars (glucose), which can be absorbed into the blood.

mcqs.q: Proteins are digested into:
mcqs.why: Proteases such as pepsin and trypsin break proteins into amino acids, their small soluble building units.

mcqs.q: The gastric glands are located in the wall of the:
mcqs.why: Gastric glands lie in the stomach wall and secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin.

mcqs.q: The enzyme that starts the digestion of proteins in the stomach is:
mcqs.why: Pepsin, present in gastric juice, begins breaking proteins into smaller pieces in the acidic medium of the stomach.

mcqs.q: The soup-like mixture of partly digested food in the stomach is called:
mcqs.why: Churning mixes food with gastric juice and turns it into a soup-like mixture called chyme, released slowly into the small intestine.

mcqs.q: Bile is secreted by the:
mcqs.why: Bile is produced by the liver, the largest gland of the body; the gall bladder only stores it and releases it when needed.

mcqs.q: Pancreatic juice is poured into the:
mcqs.why: The pancreas pours its juice into the small intestine, where its enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

lessons.title: Absorption of Digested Food
lessons.notes_html:
Villi

The inner wall of the small intestine carries millions of tiny finger-like projections called villi. They greatly increase the surface area, so digested food is absorbed quickly and in large quantity. Each villus has a network of blood capillaries, through which glucose and amino acids enter the blood, and a lacteal for absorbing fatty acids and glycerol.

Role of Bile in Fat Digestion

The gall bladder, a small sac under the liver, stores bile and releases it into the small intestine when fatty food arrives. Bile breaks large fat drops into small droplets; this is called emulsification, and it lets the enzyme lipase digest fats easily. The enzyme sucrase digests a carbohydrate (sucrose sugar).

The Large Intestine

The large intestine absorbs water and salts from the undigested food, making the waste semi-solid. Useful bacteria living here make some vitamins. The faeces are stored in the rectum and removed through the anus.

Key Points

  • Digested food is absorbed through the villi of the small intestine.
  • The gall bladder stores bile made by the liver.
  • Bile emulsifies fats; lipase then digests them.
  • The large intestine absorbs water and salts.

mcqs.q: Finger-like projections in the lining of the small intestine are called:
mcqs.why: Villi are millions of tiny finger-like projections on the inner wall of the small intestine that absorb digested food.

mcqs.q: Digested food is absorbed into the blood through the walls of:
mcqs.why: The walls of the villi absorb digested food: glucose and amino acids pass into their blood capillaries.

mcqs.q: Water and salts from undigested food are absorbed through the walls of the:
mcqs.why: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from the undigested material, turning the waste into semi-solid faeces.

mcqs.q: The function of the gall bladder is to store:
mcqs.why: The gall bladder is a small sac under the liver that stores the bile produced by the liver and releases it for fat digestion.

mcqs.q: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the ________ of a villus.
mcqs.why: Each villus has a lacteal (a lymph vessel) that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol, while its capillaries absorb glucose and amino acids.

mcqs.q: The breaking of large fat drops into small droplets by bile is called:
mcqs.why: Emulsification is the physical breaking of big fat drops into tiny droplets by bile, giving enzymes a larger surface to act on.

mcqs.q: The food digested by the enzyme sucrase belongs to:
mcqs.why: Sucrase acts on sucrose, which is a carbohydrate (sugar), so sucrase is a carbohydrate-digesting enzyme.

mcqs.q: Villi increase the surface area of the small intestine, which helps in:
options: Quick and large absorption of food
mcqs.why: Millions of villi provide a huge surface, so digested food is absorbed quickly and in large quantity into the blood.

mcqs.q: Faeces are stored in the ________ before removal from the body.
mcqs.why: After water absorption in the large intestine, the semi-solid waste (faeces) is stored in the rectum and removed through the anus.

mcqs.q: Useful bacteria living in the large intestine help by:
mcqs.why: The large intestine hosts useful bacteria that make some vitamins, which the body can then absorb and use.

lessons.title: Enzymes and Digestive Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes at Work

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up the digestion of food without being used up. Each enzyme acts on one type of food: amylase digests starch, proteases (pepsin, trypsin) digest proteins, and lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes work best at body temperature, in a suitable medium — acidic in the stomach and alkaline in the small intestine. Digestion can even occur outside the body where enzymes are provided, as in biodetergents and the food industry.

Diarrhoea and Constipation

Diarrhoea is the frequent passing of loose, watery stools, caused by germs in food or water; the patient loses water and salts and should be given ORS (oral rehydration solution). Constipation is difficulty in passing hard, dry stools; it is prevented by fibre-rich food, enough water and regular exercise.

Gas Trouble and Ulcer

Gas trouble is caused by eating too fast, overeating and spicy or fried food. An ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or intestine, caused by excess acid, bacterial infection, stress and painkiller medicines.

Key Points

  • Amylase → starch; protease → proteins; lipase → fats.
  • Enzymes speed up digestion and are not used up.
  • ORS replaces the water and salts lost in diarrhoea.
  • Fibre, water and exercise prevent constipation.

mcqs.q: The enzyme amylase digests:
mcqs.why: Amylase, present in saliva and pancreatic juice, digests starch (a carbohydrate) into sugars.

mcqs.q: Lipase digests fats into:
mcqs.why: Lipase acts in the small intestine, after bile has broken the fat into droplets, and converts fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

mcqs.q: Protease enzymes digest:
mcqs.why: Proteases such as pepsin in the stomach and trypsin in the small intestine digest proteins into amino acids.

mcqs.q: Enzymes are called biological catalysts because they:
options: Speed up digestion without being used up
mcqs.why: Like catalysts, enzymes make digestion happen much faster and come out unchanged, ready to act again.

mcqs.q: A patient suffering from diarrhoea should be given:
mcqs.why: Diarrhoea drains water and salts from the body; ORS replaces both and prevents dangerous dehydration.

mcqs.q: Constipation is prevented by:
options: Fibre-rich food, enough water and exercise
mcqs.why: Roughage (fibre) adds bulk, water keeps stools soft, and exercise keeps the gut active — together they prevent constipation.

mcqs.q: An ulcer is:
options: A sore in the lining of the stomach or intestine
mcqs.why: An ulcer is a painful sore in the inner lining of the stomach or intestine, caused by excess acid, infection, stress or painkillers.

mcqs.q: Gas trouble in the stomach is commonly caused by:
options: Eating too fast, overeating and spicy food
mcqs.why: Swallowing air while eating fast, overeating and spicy or fried food cause gas trouble, shown by belching and heaviness.

mcqs.q: Digestive enzymes work best at:
mcqs.why: Enzymes are made for the body, so they work best at body temperature and in their proper medium — acid in the stomach, alkaline in the intestine.

mcqs.q: Biodetergents clean stains better because they contain:
mcqs.why: Biodetergents contain proteases, amylases and lipases that break protein, starch and fat stains into soluble pieces.

lessons.title: Particles in Solids, Liquids and Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Everything Is Made of Particles

All matter is made of tiny particles. The behaviour of a substance depends on how its particles are arranged and how strongly they attract each other.

Solids

In solids, particles are packed very closely in a regular pattern and held by strong forces of attraction. They can only vibrate about fixed positions, so solids have a fixed shape and volume, do not flow, do not take the shape of their container, and cannot be compressed easily.

Liquids

In liquids, particles are close together but not in a regular order, and the forces between them are weaker. They can slide over one another, so a liquid flows, has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Examples: water, milk, cooking oil, petrol, honey.

Gases

In gases, particles are far apart and move freely in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape or volume; it spreads out to fill the whole container and can be compressed easily. Examples: oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen and water vapour.

Key Points

  • Solids: closely packed particles, strong forces, fixed shape.
  • Liquids: particles slide over each other; fixed volume only.
  • Gases: particles far apart; no fixed shape or volume.
  • Solids and liquids cannot be compressed easily.

mcqs.q: Strong forces of attraction between particles are present in:
mcqs.why: In solids the particles are held tightly by strong forces of attraction, so they keep fixed positions and the solid keeps its shape.

mcqs.q: Solids and liquids cannot be compressed easily as their particles are:
mcqs.why: Their particles are already closely packed with little empty space between them, so pressing cannot squeeze them much smaller.

mcqs.q: The materials that do not take the shape of the container are:
mcqs.why: Solids keep their own shape wherever they are placed; liquids and gases take the shape of the container holding them.

mcqs.q: Solids have fixed shape and volume because their particles:
options: Are locked in fixed positions and only vibrate
mcqs.why: Strong attraction locks solid particles in a regular pattern; they only vibrate in place, so shape and volume stay fixed.

mcqs.q: In a liquid, the particles:
options: Are in a fixed regular pattern
mcqs.why: Liquid particles are close but free to slide past each other, which is why liquids flow and take the container's shape.

mcqs.q: A gas spreads out to fill the whole container because its particles:
mcqs.why: Gas particles are far apart and move freely at high speed in every direction, so the gas expands to fill all available space.

mcqs.q: When a solid is cooled further, it:
options: Remains a solid and usually contracts
mcqs.why: Cooling a solid only makes its particles vibrate less and the solid contracts slightly; it is already in the lowest-energy state.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a gas at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Oxygen is a gas at room temperature; water, milk and honey are liquids with fixed volume but no fixed shape.

mcqs.q: A liquid has:
options: No fixed shape but fixed volume
No fixed shape and no fixed volume
Fixed shape but no fixed volume
mcqs.why: Liquid particles slide over one another, so a liquid flows into the container's shape, but the amount (volume) stays the same.

mcqs.q: Why do solids not flow like liquids and gases?
options: Their particles are locked in fixed positions by strong forces
mcqs.why: Flowing needs particles to change places; in solids, strong forces lock particles in fixed positions, so solids cannot flow.

lessons.title: Changing the State of Matter
lessons.notes_html:
Heating and Cooling

We change the physical state of matter by heating or cooling. Heating gives energy to the particles: when a solid is heated, its particles vibrate faster until it melts. Cooling removes energy, so particles slow down and come closer.

The Changes of State

Melting: solid changes into liquid on heating (ice into water at 0°C). Freezing: liquid changes into solid on cooling (water into ice at 0°C) and gives out heat. Boiling: liquid changes into gas throughout the liquid at its boiling point (100°C for water). Condensation: gas changes into liquid on cooling — the opposite of boiling. Evaporation: liquid changes into gas from its surface at any temperature. Sublimation: a solid changes directly into gas on heating, without becoming liquid, as with camphor, iodine and dry ice.

The Substance Stays the Same

These are physical changes: ice, water and steam are all the same substance — water — in different states.

Key Points

  • Gas → liquid is condensation; solid → gas directly is sublimation.
  • Water boils at 100°C and ice melts at 0°C.
  • Melting takes in heat; freezing gives out heat.
  • Evaporation happens from the surface at any temperature.

mcqs.q: The process of changing a gas into a liquid is called:
mcqs.why: Condensation is the change of a gas into a liquid on cooling, e.g. steam forming water drops on a cold lid.

mcqs.q: The process of changing a solid directly into the gaseous state on heating is called:
mcqs.why: In sublimation a solid skips the liquid state and becomes gas directly, as camphor and dry ice do on heating.

mcqs.q: When a gas condenses, it becomes:
mcqs.why: Condensation turns a gas into a liquid as its particles lose energy and come closer together on cooling.

mcqs.q: When a solid is heated, its particles begin to:
mcqs.why: Heating gives energy to the particles of a solid, so they vibrate faster and faster until the solid melts.

mcqs.q: The boiling point of water is:
mcqs.why: Water boils at 100°C at normal air pressure, changing throughout the liquid into vapour (gas).

mcqs.q: The process opposite to boiling is:
mcqs.why: Boiling turns a liquid into a gas by heating; condensation is the reverse — a gas turning into a liquid by cooling.

mcqs.q: Ice changes into water at:
mcqs.why: Ice melts at 0°C, and at the same temperature water freezes into ice; 0°C is both the melting and freezing point of water.

mcqs.q: Freezing is a process in which:
options: Heat is taken in by the liquid
A gas becomes a solid directly
A liquid gives out heat and becomes a solid
mcqs.why: When a liquid freezes, its particles lose energy (heat is given out) and arrange into the fixed pattern of a solid.

mcqs.q: Which of these substances shows sublimation?
mcqs.why: Camphor pieces slowly disappear into vapour without melting — a direct solid-to-gas change called sublimation.

mcqs.q: Evaporation takes place:
options: From the surface of a liquid at any temperature
mcqs.why: Evaporation is a surface process: particles escape from the surface of a liquid at any temperature, e.g. wet clothes drying.

lessons.title: Diffusion and Changes of State in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Diffusion

Diffusion is the movement of particles from where they are more (higher concentration) to where they are less, until they spread evenly — for example, the smell of perfume spreading through a room, or a drop of ink colouring a glass of water. Diffusion is fastest in gases, slower in liquids and almost absent in solids. It is the opposite of compression, which pushes particles together into a smaller volume.

Steam and Water Vapour

Water vapour in the air is a true invisible gas. The white cloud we call steam is actually tiny liquid droplets formed when hot vapour condenses in cooler air. After sunset, only water vapour condenses as dew, because it alone is near its condensation point at ordinary temperatures.

Uses in Daily Life

Freezing preserves food, meat and medicines. Boiling cooks food and kills germs in water. Evaporation dries clothes, cools water in an earthen pot and cools our skin as sweat; salt is obtained from sea water by evaporation. Condensation gives distilled water, dew and rain. Melting is used for candles, ghee, and shaping metals and glass.

Factors Affecting Evaporation

Evaporation is faster with higher temperature, larger surface area, wind, and lower humidity; diffusion is faster at higher temperature and with lighter particles.

Key Points

  • Diffusion spreads particles from more to less concentrated regions.
  • Dew is condensed water vapour on cold surfaces.
  • Evaporation from a matka keeps drinking water cool.
  • Heating a gas makes its particles move faster and the gas expand.

mcqs.q: Movement of particles from where they are more to where they are less is called:
mcqs.why: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration until they are even.

mcqs.q: The smell of perfume spreading throughout a room is an example of:
mcqs.why: Perfume particles move from the bottle area (more concentrated) to the whole room (less concentrated) — this is diffusion in a gas.

mcqs.q: After sunset, dew forms because:
options: Only water vapour is near its condensation point and condenses on cold surfaces
mcqs.why: Cold grass cools the air touching it; only water vapour can condense at ordinary temperatures, so it alone forms dew drops.

mcqs.q: The white cloud called steam above boiling water is visible because:
options: It is made of tiny liquid droplets that scatter light
It is made of ice crystals
mcqs.why: True water vapour is invisible; the white cloud is tiny condensed water droplets, and these droplets scatter light so we see them.

mcqs.q: Freezing is used in daily life to:
mcqs.why: In freezers, low temperature stops germs from growing, so food, meat, vaccines and medicines stay fresh for a long time.

mcqs.q: Water kept in an earthen pot (matka) stays cool because of:
mcqs.why: Water oozes through the pot's pores and evaporates from its surface; evaporation takes heat from the water inside, keeping it cool.

mcqs.q: Common salt is obtained from sea water by:
mcqs.why: Sea water is left in shallow pans; the sun evaporates the water and the dissolved salt is left behind as crystals.

mcqs.q: Clothes dry faster on a windy day because wind:
mcqs.why: Wind blows away the vapour near the clothes, so more water can evaporate; evaporation also speeds up with heat and large surface area.

mcqs.q: Diffusion is fastest in:
mcqs.why: Gas particles move freely and quickly, so diffusion is fastest in gases, slower in liquids and extremely slow in solids.

mcqs.q: When a gas is heated, its particles:
options: Gain energy, move faster and spread farther apart
mcqs.why: Heating gives gas particles energy; they move faster and farther apart, so the gas expands and its pressure rises in a closed container.

lessons.title: Elements — Metals, Non-metals and Metalloids
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Element?

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atoms, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical methods. There are 118 known elements, such as hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), carbon (C), iron (Fe) and gold (Au).

Metals

Metals are hard, shiny (lustrous), malleable and ductile, and good conductors of heat and electricity — for example iron (Fe), copper (Cu), aluminium (Al), gold (Au) and silver (Ag). Lithium, sodium and potassium are also metals.

Non-metals and Metalloids

Non-metals are generally dull, brittle and poor conductors — for example oxygen (O), hydrogen (H), carbon (C), sulphur (S), nitrogen (N) and chlorine (Cl). Metalloids, such as boron (B) and silicon (Si), show properties of both metals and non-metals and are used in electronics.

Noble Gases

The noble gases — helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar) — are very unreactive elements that exist as single atoms. Helium fills balloons, neon is used in sign tubes, and argon is filled in electric bulbs.

Key Points

  • An element has only one kind of atoms; 118 are known.
  • Iron = Fe, Copper = Cu, Gold = Au, Silver = Ag.
  • Boron and silicon are metalloids.
  • Noble gases are unreactive and monoatomic.

mcqs.q: Which one is a metallic element?
mcqs.why: Lithium is a metal (like sodium and potassium); chlorine, sulphur and bromine are non-metallic elements.

mcqs.q: Which one is a non-metallic element?
mcqs.why: Oxygen is a non-metal gas; lithium, sodium and potassium are all soft metals of the same family.

mcqs.q: Which one is a metalloid?
mcqs.why: Boron shows properties of both metals and non-metals, so it is a metalloid; silicon is another common metalloid.

mcqs.q: An element is a pure substance made of:
mcqs.why: By definition an element contains only one kind of atoms and cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical methods.

mcqs.q: The chemical symbol of iron is:
mcqs.why: Iron's symbol Fe comes from its Latin name ferrum; symbols are not always the first letters of the English name.

mcqs.q: The chemical symbol of copper is:
mcqs.why: Copper has the symbol Cu, from its Latin name cuprum; Co is cobalt and Cr is chromium.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a noble gas?
mcqs.why: Neon is a noble gas — very unreactive and existing as single atoms; it is used in advertising sign tubes and lights.

mcqs.q: Metals are generally good conductors of:
mcqs.why: Metals like copper and aluminium conduct heat and electricity well, which is why copper is used for electric wires.

mcqs.q: Non-metals are generally:
mcqs.why: Non-metals such as sulphur and carbon are dull, brittle (not malleable) and poor conductors of heat and electricity.

mcqs.q: The total number of known elements is:
mcqs.why: Scientists have so far identified 118 elements, from hydrogen (H) to the heaviest synthetic elements in the periodic table.

lessons.title: Atoms and Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
Atom

An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. An atom has a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. A helium atom, for example, has 2 neutrons in its nucleus.

Molecule

A molecule is formed when two or more atoms join together; it is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently. A molecule of two atoms, like O2, is called diatomic.

Monoatomic and Polyatomic Molecules

A monoatomic molecule consists of a single atom existing independently — the noble gases helium (He) and neon (Ne), which can exist alone at room temperature. A polyatomic molecule has three or more atoms joined together, such as ozone (O3) and methane (CH4).

Key Points

  • Atom: smallest particle of an element in a reaction.
  • Molecule: two or more atoms joined together.
  • Noble gases exist as single atoms (monoatomic).
  • O2 is diatomic; O3 is polyatomic.

mcqs.q: Which atom can exist independently at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Neon is a noble gas; its atoms are stable alone, so Ne exists independently, while H, Cl and O join into molecules like H2, Cl2 and O2.

mcqs.q: How many atoms are present in one molecule of helium?
mcqs.why: Helium is monoatomic — each 'molecule' of helium is a single atom, written simply as He.

mcqs.q: The number of neutrons in a helium atom is:
mcqs.why: A helium nucleus contains 2 protons and 2 neutrons, with 2 electrons moving around the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction is the:
mcqs.why: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction; molecules are groups of atoms.

mcqs.q: A molecule made of exactly two atoms, such as O2, is called:
mcqs.why: Diatomic means two atoms per molecule; O2, H2 and N2 are diatomic molecules of their elements.

mcqs.q: An ozone molecule (O3) contains:
mcqs.why: The small number 3 in O3 shows three oxygen atoms joined in one molecule, so ozone is a polyatomic molecule.

mcqs.q: Noble gases exist as:
mcqs.why: Noble gases are monoatomic: each particle is one single atom, because these gases are unreactive and do not join with others.

mcqs.q: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that:
options: Can take part in a reaction
Can be seen with the eye
mcqs.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and still show the substance's properties.

mcqs.q: Which of these exists as a single atom?
mcqs.why: Helium (He) is a noble gas and exists as single atoms; O2 and H2 are diatomic molecules and CO2 is a compound molecule.

mcqs.q: Atoms join together to form:
mcqs.why: When two or more atoms join together they form a molecule, such as two hydrogen atoms forming an H2 molecule.

lessons.title: Reading Chemical Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
What a Formula Tells Us

A chemical formula shows which elements are present in a substance and how many atoms of each are in one molecule. The small number written after a symbol counts the atoms of that element: in NH3 (ammonia) there is 1 nitrogen atom and 3 hydrogen atoms; in C6H12O6 (glucose) there are 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms.

Elements and Compounds by Formula

A formula with only one kind of atom is an element: N2 (2 atoms), O2 (2 atoms), O3 (3 atoms). A formula with two or more different elements is a compound: H2O (3 atoms: 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen), CO2 (3 atoms: 1 carbon + 2 oxygen). Water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and methane are compounds; hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are elements. A picture model showing two different atoms joined together indicates a compound.

Common Compounds

Water — H2O; carbon dioxide — CO2; ammonia — NH3; methane — CH4; glucose — C6H12O6; common salt — NaCl. A compound can be broken into its elements only by chemical methods.

Key Points

  • The subscript number counts atoms of the element before it.
  • One kind of atom in the formula = element; different kinds = compound.
  • NH3 has 3 hydrogen atoms; glucose has 6 oxygen atoms.
  • Common salt has the formula NaCl.

mcqs.q: How many hydrogen atoms are present in one molecule of ammonia (NH3)?
mcqs.why: In NH3, the subscript 3 after H means three hydrogen atoms joined with one nitrogen atom in each ammonia molecule.

mcqs.q: C6H12O6 is the chemical formula of glucose. How many oxygen atoms are present in glucose?
mcqs.why: The subscript after O in C6H12O6 is 6, so each glucose molecule contains 6 oxygen atoms (and 6 carbon and 12 hydrogen atoms).

mcqs.q: Which one is an element?
mcqs.why: O3 contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element; CO2, H2O and NH3 each contain two different elements, so they are compounds.

mcqs.q: Water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and methane are:
mcqs.why: Each of these is made of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, so all four are compounds.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are:
mcqs.why: Each of these substances is made of only one kind of atoms, which is the definition of an element.

mcqs.q: A picture showing two different atoms joined together (a model) indicates:
mcqs.why: Different atoms chemically joined in one molecule means a compound, because a compound contains two or more different elements combined.

mcqs.q: How many atoms are present in total in one molecule of CO2?
mcqs.why: CO2 has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms, so the total number of atoms in one molecule is 1 + 2 = 3.

mcqs.q: The elements present in H2O are:
mcqs.why: The formula H2O shows 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen combined in every molecule of water.

mcqs.q: A compound can be broken down into its elements:
mcqs.why: In a compound the elements are chemically combined, so only chemical methods — not physical ones like filtration — can separate them.

mcqs.q: The chemical formula of common salt is:
mcqs.why: Common salt is sodium chloride, written NaCl: one atom of sodium (Na) joined with one atom of chlorine (Cl).

lessons.title: Mixtures and Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Mixtures

A mixture is formed when two or more substances are physically mixed in any ratio; they keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods. In a homogeneous mixture the components are uniformly mixed and cannot be seen separately — for example salt solution, air, steel and vinegar. In a heterogeneous mixture the components are not uniform and can be seen — for example sand in water, oil in water, chalk in water and soil.

Solutions

A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which one substance dissolves uniformly in another. The substance dissolved (in smaller amount) is the solute, and the substance in which it dissolves (in larger amount) is the solvent: solute + solvent = solution. In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. Water is called the universal solvent. Brass is a solid solution of copper and zinc.

Alloys

Alloys are homogeneous mixtures (solid solutions) of metals: steel (iron + carbon), brass (copper + zinc) and bronze (copper + tin). In air, nitrogen is regarded as the solvent because it is present in the largest amount (about 78%).

Key Points

  • Solutions are homogeneous mixtures with solute + solvent.
  • Steel, brass and bronze are alloys (solid solutions).
  • Sand in water is heterogeneous; salt in water is homogeneous.
  • In air, nitrogen (78%) acts as the solvent.

mcqs.q: Which one is matter?
mcqs.why: Matter has mass and occupies space; rain is water, which is matter, while light, heat and shadow are forms of energy or effects, not matter.

mcqs.q: Which one is a mixture?
mcqs.why: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other gases physically mixed in no fixed ratio.

mcqs.q: Which one is a homogeneous mixture?
mcqs.why: Steel is a uniform mixture of iron and carbon throughout; sand, oil and chalk do not mix uniformly with water, so they are heterogeneous.

mcqs.q: Which one is a solution?
mcqs.why: Brass is a solid solution — a homogeneous mixture in which copper and zinc are uniformly mixed; milk, blood and smoke are not uniform solutions.

mcqs.q: In a salt solution, the solute is:
mcqs.why: The solute is the substance that dissolves, present in smaller amount; in salt solution, salt dissolves in water, the solvent.

mcqs.q: Water is called the universal solvent because:
mcqs.why: Water dissolves a very large number of substances — salts, sugar, gases and many more — so it is called the universal solvent.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
mcqs.why: In sand and water the components are not uniformly mixed and the sand can be seen separately and settles, so it is heterogeneous.

mcqs.q: Alloys are:
mcqs.why: Alloys like steel, brass and bronze are homogeneous mixtures (solid solutions) of two or more metals, or a metal with a non-metal.

mcqs.q: Bronze is an alloy of copper and:
mcqs.why: Bronze is made by mixing copper with tin; it is used for statues, medals and coins. Brass is copper with zinc instead.

mcqs.q: In air, the solvent is considered to be:
mcqs.why: The solvent is the component present in the largest amount; nitrogen forms about 78% of air, so it is the solvent of air.

lessons.title: Separating the Parts of a Mixture
lessons.notes_html:
Separation Techniques

The components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods. Crystallization obtains pure solid crystals from a saturated solution by cooling or evaporation. Chromatography separates the coloured components of a mixture, such as ink dyes, as they move at different speeds through paper.

Separating Immiscible Liquids

Liquids that do not mix, like oil and water, are separated with a separating funnel. The mixture is left to stand: the denser liquid (water) settles at the bottom and the lighter one (oil) floats on top. The tap is opened to run out the lower layer, and closed just before the boundary reaches it.

Fractional Distillation and Solubility

Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation: petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and bitumen left at the bottom. Tests show that common salt, sugar, glucose and copper sulphate are soluble in water, while chalk powder, iodine, oil and grease are insoluble.

Key Points

  • Chromatography separates coloured components of a mixture.
  • A separating funnel separates oil and water.
  • Bitumen is the last fraction left in fractional distillation.
  • Chalk is insoluble in water; sugar is soluble.

mcqs.q: The technique used for the separation of coloured components of a mixture is called:
mcqs.why: Chromatography separates coloured components, like the dyes in ink, as they travel at different speeds through paper.

mcqs.q: Pure solid crystals of a substance are obtained from its saturated solution by:
mcqs.why: In crystallization, a saturated solution is cooled or evaporated so that pure crystals of the dissolved solid form and can be collected.

mcqs.q: Oil and water can be separated by using a:
mcqs.why: Oil and water are immiscible; in a separating funnel the denser water settles below the oil and is run out through the tap.

mcqs.q: In a separating funnel containing oil and water, the liquid that settles at the bottom is:
mcqs.why: Water is denser than oil, so it settles in the lower layer while the lighter oil floats on top, ready to be separated.

mcqs.q: Crude oil is separated into its fractions by:
mcqs.why: Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions with different boiling points, from petroleum gas at the top to bitumen at the bottom.

mcqs.q: The fraction left at the bottom in the fractional distillation of crude oil is:
mcqs.why: Bitumen (tar) has the highest boiling point, so it remains at the bottom of the fractionating column and is used for making roads.

mcqs.q: Chalk powder mixed in water:
options: Forms a cloudy suspension and settles
mcqs.why: Chalk is insoluble in water; it makes the water cloudy and slowly settles at the bottom as a suspension.

mcqs.q: Which of these substances is soluble in water?
mcqs.why: Sugar disappears into water forming a clear solution, so it is soluble; chalk, oil and grease do not dissolve in water.

mcqs.q: The components of a mixture can be separated by:
mcqs.why: In a mixture the substances are only physically mixed, so filtration, evaporation, magnets and similar physical methods can separate them.

mcqs.q: Iodine in water is:
mcqs.why: Iodine hardly dissolves in water at all, so in the solubility test it is recorded as almost insoluble in water.

lessons.title: Compounds, Mixtures and the Air Around Us
lessons.notes_html:
Compound or Mixture?

In a compound, elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio by mass; it has new, fixed properties and can be separated only by chemical methods. Sugar is a compound, not an element. An element is composed of atoms and has fixed properties, but it cannot be decomposed by chemical methods or by heating.

Air Is a Mixture

Air contains the elements nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%) with noble gases, and the compounds carbon dioxide and water vapour. Its impurities include dust, smoke and harmful gases from vehicles and factories. Nitrogen dilutes oxygen and is needed by plants to make proteins; carbon dioxide is used by plants for photosynthesis; oxygen is needed for respiration and burning.

Underground Water

Underground water is a mixture of dissolved minerals and gases with suspended sand, mud and germs. For drinking, it is passed through layers of cloth, sand and gravel to filter it, and then boiled to kill germs.

Key Points

  • A compound has a fixed ratio by mass; a mixture has any ratio.
  • Sugar is a compound, not an element.
  • Air: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, plus CO2 and water vapour.
  • Filter and boil underground water before drinking.

mcqs.q: Which one is different from the others?
mcqs.why: Ice, water and steam are the three states of the same substance (water), while sodium is a completely different substance — an element.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true for a compound?
options: It is a substance of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio by mass
It is always a mixture of elements
It cannot be a pure substance
mcqs.why: A compound always contains its elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio by mass, e.g. water always has hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:8 by mass.

mcqs.q: Which one is not an element?
mcqs.why: Sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; sodium, calcium and oxygen are elements made of one kind of atoms.

mcqs.q: Which one is a non-metal?
mcqs.why: Phosphorus is a non-metal element; sodium, calcium and magnesium are all metals.

mcqs.q: Which statement is false?
options: An element is composed of atoms
An element can be decomposed by chemical methods
An element is a pure substance
mcqs.why: An element cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical methods or by heating — that is what makes it an element.

mcqs.q: The percentage of nitrogen in air is about:
mcqs.why: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with about 1% carbon dioxide, noble gases and water vapour.

mcqs.q: Plants use carbon dioxide from the air for:
mcqs.why: Green plants take in carbon dioxide and use it, with water and sunlight, to prepare their food by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Oxygen in the air is necessary for:
mcqs.why: All living things use oxygen for respiration to release energy from food, and burning (combustion) also cannot take place without oxygen.

mcqs.q: Underground water can be filtered for drinking by passing it through layers of:
mcqs.why: Layers of cloth, sand and gravel trap the suspended sand, mud and germs; the filtered water is then boiled to make it fully safe.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an air pollutant?
mcqs.why: Smoke, dust and harmful gases like carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide from vehicles and factories pollute the air.

lessons.title: Forms of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Energy and Its Forms

Energy is the ability to do work. It exists in many forms: kinetic energy (energy of moving things), heat, light, sound, electrical and chemical energy. The temperature of an object is the measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles.

Stored (Potential) Energy

Stored energy is also called potential energy. Chemical energy is stored in food, fuels and batteries — our food is a source of chemical energy. Gravitational potential energy is stored in an object due to its height, like water in a dam or a fruit hanging on a tree; when the fruit falls, this energy changes into kinetic energy. Elastic potential energy is stored in a stretched rubber band or a wound spring.

Energy Converters

Devices that change energy from one form to another are energy converters: a fan, a bulb and a motor are converters, while a table is not. A catapult converts elastic potential energy into kinetic energy of the stone; a tree converts light energy into chemical energy in food; a burner converts chemical energy of fuel into heat and light.

Key Points

  • Temperature measures the kinetic energy of particles.
  • Food and fuels store chemical energy.
  • Energy stored due to height is gravitational potential energy.
  • A table is not an energy converter; a fan, bulb and motor are.

mcqs.q: Temperature of an object is the measure of ________ of its particles.
mcqs.why: Temperature tells how fast the particles of an object are moving on average, so it measures their average kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: While drilling a hole, the useful form of kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: The drill's useful output is the mechanical (movement) work of the rotating bit cutting the hole; heat and sound are wasted forms.

mcqs.q: Our food is a source of:
mcqs.why: Food stores chemical energy, which our body releases during respiration to do work, grow and keep warm.

mcqs.q: When a fruit is detached from the tree stalk, the energy it possesses due to its position is converted into:
mcqs.why: The hanging fruit has gravitational potential energy due to its height; as it falls, that energy changes into kinetic energy of motion.

mcqs.q: The energy stored in a stretched rubber band is:
mcqs.why: A stretched or compressed object stores elastic potential energy, which is released as movement when the object is let go.

mcqs.q: Water stored in a dam has:
mcqs.why: Water held at a height in a dam stores gravitational potential energy, which is later changed into kinetic and then electrical energy.

mcqs.q: In a catapult, the main energy conversion is:
options: Elastic potential energy into kinetic energy
mcqs.why: The stretched band of the catapult stores elastic potential energy, which changes into kinetic energy of the flying stone when released.

mcqs.q: A tree (during photosynthesis) converts:
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis a tree traps light (solar) energy and stores it as chemical energy in the food it prepares.

mcqs.q: A gas burner converts chemical energy of the fuel into:
mcqs.why: Burning gas releases its stored chemical energy as heat (for cooking) and light (the flame).

mcqs.q: While blowing up a balloon, the kinetic energy of the blown air is converted into:
options: Elastic potential (strain) energy of the stretched rubber
mcqs.why: The blown air stretches the rubber of the balloon, so its kinetic energy is stored as elastic potential (strain) energy in the rubber.

lessons.title: Energy Conversion and Conservation
lessons.notes_html:
Law of Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form into another. During any conversion, the total amount of energy always remains the same. (Note: the book's printed answer key for this point is wrong — energy is never destroyed.)

Dissipated (Wasted) Energy

During conversions, some energy spreads into the surroundings as heat and sound and cannot be used again. This is called dissipated energy or wasted energy — for example, a bouncing ball gradually converts its energy into heat and sound at each bounce until it stops; the energy is not lost, only changed into forms we cannot use.

Everyday Conversions

A child kicking a football: chemical energy of muscles → kinetic energy of the ball. A person walking upstairs: chemical energy → gravitational potential energy.
