Water boiled in a kettle: electrical energy → heat energy. A glowing bulb: electrical energy → light energy and some heat. A dynamo converts mechanical (kinetic) energy into electrical energy.

Key Points

  • Energy is never created or destroyed — only converted.
  • The total energy in every conversion remains the same.
  • Energy spread out as heat and sound is called wasted energy.
  • A dynamo changes mechanical energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: During work done, energy is:
mcqs.why: Whenever work is done, energy changes from one form into another; it is neither created nor destroyed in the process.

mcqs.q: Which one is not an energy converter?
mcqs.why: A fan, bulb and motor all change energy from one form to another; a table does not convert energy, so it is not a converter.

mcqs.q: The engine of a vehicle starts working using:
mcqs.why: The starter motor of a vehicle runs on electrical energy from the battery to turn and start the engine.

mcqs.q: During energy conversion, the total amount of energy:
mcqs.why: By the law of conservation of energy, energy is never created or destroyed in a conversion, so the total amount always remains the same. (The book's printed key wrongly says 'destroyed'.)

mcqs.q: Dissipated energy is called wasted energy because it:
options: Spreads into the surroundings as heat and sound and cannot be used again
mcqs.why: Dissipated energy escapes into the surroundings, usually as heat and sound, and cannot be collected for useful work, so it is called wasted.

mcqs.q: A dynamo converts:
mcqs.why: In a dynamo, a rotating coil's mechanical (kinetic) energy is converted into electrical energy, e.g. in a bicycle dynamo or a generator.

mcqs.q: A bouncing ball finally stops. According to the law of conservation of energy, its energy:
options: Was converted into heat, sound and shape-changing energy
mcqs.why: Energy is never destroyed; at each bounce the ball's energy changed into heat (friction), sound and a little energy of changing shape.

mcqs.q: The main energy transfer in a glowing bulb is:
options: Electrical energy into light energy (and some heat)
mcqs.why: A bulb changes electrical energy mainly into light energy, with some energy wasted as heat — which is why bulbs feel warm.

mcqs.q: When a person walks upstairs, chemical energy of the body changes into:
mcqs.why: Climbing raises the body to a greater height, so the chemical energy from food is stored as gravitational potential energy.

mcqs.q: In riding a bicycle, the rider's muscles convert chemical energy from food into:
options: Kinetic energy of the pedals and wheels
mcqs.why: The rider's muscles change the chemical energy of food into kinetic (mechanical) energy, which the pedals, chain and wheels use to move the bicycle.

lessons.title: Sources of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Renewable and Non-renewable Sources

Renewable sources of energy can be used again and again and will not finish — for example wind, sunlight, water and biogas. Non-renewable sources like coal, natural gas and oil were formed over millions of years and will run out one day; they also store chemical energy, like food, fuels and batteries.

Biogas

Biogas is a mixture of gases formed by the decay of animal waste (dung) in the absence of air. It can be burnt as a fuel for cooking and lighting in villages.

Where Dynamo Energy Comes From

The electrical energy produced by a dynamo comes from mechanical energy: its coil is rotated by a bicycle wheel, flowing water, wind or an engine.

Potential Energy Depends on Height

An experiment dropping a metal sphere on sand from 5, 10, 15 and 20 cm shows that the pit is largest from the greatest height: the greater the height, the greater the gravitational potential energy.

Key Points

  • Wind is a renewable source; coal, oil and gas are not.
  • Biogas is produced by the decay of animal waste.
  • A dynamo's electricity comes from mechanical energy.
  • Potential energy increases with height.

mcqs.q: Which is a renewable source of energy?
mcqs.why: Wind is renewable — it is replaced naturally and will not finish; coal, natural gas and oil are non-renewable fossil fuels.

mcqs.q: A mixture of gases formed by the decay of animal waste is called:
mcqs.why: Biogas is produced when animal waste (dung) decays without air; it is a useful fuel gas in villages.

mcqs.q: The electrical energy produced by a dynamo comes from:
mcqs.why: A dynamo's coil is rotated — by a wheel, water, wind or an engine — and this mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: Which of these sources of energy will run out one day with use?
mcqs.why: Coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years; the stock in the earth is limited and will finish, unlike wind or sunlight.

mcqs.q: In the sand-pit experiment, the sphere dropped from the greatest height makes the largest pit because it has:
mcqs.why: Potential energy depends on height: the sphere at 20 cm has the most gravitational potential energy, so it makes the biggest pit.

mcqs.q: Biogas is mainly produced from:
mcqs.why: Biogas forms when animal waste decays in a closed tank without air; the gas produced can be burnt for cooking and lighting.

mcqs.q: Chemical energy is stored in:
mcqs.why: Food, fuels like petrol and coal, and batteries all store chemical energy, which is released when they are used or burnt.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a non-renewable source of energy?
mcqs.why: Natural gas is a fossil fuel with a limited stock underground, so it is non-renewable; wind, sunlight and biogas keep renewing.

mcqs.q: A wound-up spring of a toy car stores:
mcqs.why: Winding the spring squeezes it, storing elastic potential energy, which changes into kinetic energy when the toy car is released.

mcqs.q: The pit made by dropping a sphere from 5 cm height on sand is:
mcqs.why: From the smallest height the sphere has the least potential energy, so it makes the smallest pit in the sand.

lessons.title: Electric Charge and Static Electricity
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Charge

Charge is a basic property of particles of matter. It is of two types: positive charge, carried by protons, and negative charge, carried by electrons. An object becomes charged when it gains or loses electrons. The rule of charges is: like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract each other.

Static Electricity

Static electricity is the charge that builds up on the surface of an object when it is rubbed with another object, and stays there without flowing. A plastic comb rubbed with dry hair attracts small pieces of paper. Static charge is not used in domestic wiring, but it is useful in photocopiers and laser printers, in spray painting, and in removing smoke particles from chimneys.

Lightning

Lightning is static electricity on a huge scale. In a thunderstorm, rubbing water drops and ice make the clouds charged; when the charge becomes very large, it suddenly discharges through the air as a bright flash, with the loud sound of thunder. A lightning conductor carries this charge safely to the ground.

Key Points

  • Protons are positively charged; electrons are negatively charged.
  • Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
  • Static electricity is produced by rubbing (friction).
  • Lightning is a giant discharge of static electricity.

mcqs.q: The positively charged particle is the:
mcqs.why: A proton carries a positive charge, an electron carries a negative charge, and a neutron carries no charge at all.

mcqs.q: Like charges:
mcqs.why: Two positive charges repel each other, and two negative charges also repel; only unlike charges (positive and negative) attract.

mcqs.q: Unlike charges (a positive and a negative):
mcqs.why: A positively charged object and a negatively charged object pull towards each other — unlike charges attract.

mcqs.q: Static electricity is produced by:
mcqs.why: Rubbing (friction) transfers electrons from one object to another, leaving both charged; this stationary charge is static electricity.

mcqs.q: A plastic comb rubbed with dry hair attracts small pieces of paper because of:
mcqs.why: Rubbing charges the comb with static electricity, and this charge attracts the light, uncharged pieces of paper.

mcqs.q: Lightning is a natural example of:
options: Static electricity on a huge scale
mcqs.why: Charged clouds suddenly discharge through the air as lightning — the same static electricity as a comb spark, but enormously bigger.

mcqs.q: The loud sound heard during a thunderstorm with lightning is called:
mcqs.why: The sudden discharge of lightning heats the air violently, producing the loud sound we hear as thunder.

mcqs.q: Static electricity is mostly used in domestic wiring:
mcqs.why: Static charge does not flow continuously and cannot run appliances, so homes use current electricity from the supply instead.

mcqs.q: Static electricity is usefully applied in:
mcqs.why: Photocopiers and laser printers use static charge to attract toner powder onto the paper in the shape of the image or text.

mcqs.q: An object becomes electrically charged when it:
mcqs.why: Charging is a transfer of electrons: an object that gains electrons becomes negative, and one that loses them becomes positive.

lessons.title: Electric Circuits and Their Components
lessons.notes_html:
Current Electricity

Current electricity is the flow of electric charges (electrons) through a conductor such as a wire. It is produced by a cell, battery or generator. A cell stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy in a circuit; its chemical energy provides the push that keeps the charges moving.

Components of a Circuit

A simple electric circuit has: a source (cell or battery), connecting wires, a switch — the device used to open or close the circuit — and a device that uses electricity, such as a bulb. A fuse, ammeter and voltmeter may also be added.

Open and Closed Circuits

In a closed circuit the path is complete, current flows and the bulb glows. In an open circuit the path is broken (switch off), so no current flows.

Circuit Diagrams

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: a cell is drawn as one short and one long line, a battery as pairs of these lines, a switch as a break that can be closed, a bulb as a circle with a cross, and wires as straight lines forming a loop.

Key Points

  • A cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
  • A switch opens or closes a circuit.
  • Current flows only in a closed (complete) circuit.
  • Wires join all components into a loop.

mcqs.q: A device that stores chemical energy and converts it into electric energy in a circuit is a:
mcqs.why: A cell's chemicals store energy; in a circuit the cell converts this chemical energy into electrical energy that drives the current.

mcqs.q: The device used to open or close a circuit is a:
mcqs.why: A switch completes or breaks the circuit path: closing it lets current flow, and opening it stops the current.

mcqs.q: Current electricity is:
options: The flow of charges through a conductor
mcqs.why: Current electricity is the ordered flow of electrons through a conductor like a wire, produced by a cell, battery or generator.

mcqs.q: In an open circuit:
options: Current flows and the bulb glows
No current flows because the path is broken
mcqs.why: An open circuit has a break in the path — for example the switch is off — so charges cannot flow and the bulb stays off.

mcqs.q: In a closed circuit:
options: The path is complete and current flows
mcqs.why: A closed circuit forms a complete loop from the cell through the devices and back, so current flows and the bulb lights up.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a basic component of a simple electric circuit?
mcqs.why: A simple circuit needs a source (cell), wires, a switch and a device like a bulb; a magnet is not a circuit component.

mcqs.q: In a circuit diagram, a bulb is drawn as:
mcqs.why: By standard symbols, a bulb is shown as a circle with a cross or filament inside; a cell is a pair of short and long lines.

mcqs.q: The purpose of connecting wires in a circuit is to:
options: Join all components into a complete loop
mcqs.why: Wires are the conductors that connect the cell, switch and bulb into one loop along which the charges can flow.

mcqs.q: Which extra component protects a circuit from damage by excess current?
mcqs.why: A fuse is a safety component whose thin wire melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes dangerously large.

mcqs.q: The push that keeps charges moving in a circuit comes from:
options: The chemical energy of the cell
mcqs.why: The cell converts its stored chemical energy into electrical energy, providing the push that drives electrons through the wire.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.notes_html:
Series Circuit

In a series circuit, components are joined one after another, so current has only one path. The voltage is shared among the bulbs: adding more bulbs makes each one dimmer, while adding more cells in series increases the voltage and the bulbs glow brighter.

Parallel Circuit

In a parallel circuit, components are joined in separate branches, giving current two or more paths. Every device is connected directly across the supply, so each gets the full voltage, works independently, and if one bulb fuses the others keep glowing.

Why Homes Use Parallel Circuits

A series circuit is not suitable for homes: switching off or fusing one appliance would stop all the others, and each would get less voltage. That is why domestic (home) wiring uses parallel circuits.

Key Points

  • Series: one path; voltage shared; bulbs dim as more are added.
  • Parallel: many branches; full voltage to each device.
  • More cells in series make bulbs brighter.
  • Home wiring is parallel.

mcqs.q: The circuit which provides multiple paths for the current to flow is the:
mcqs.why: In a parallel circuit the components are connected in separate branches, so the current has several paths to flow through.

mcqs.q: The type of circuit used in domestic (home) wiring is the:
mcqs.why: Homes use parallel wiring so that every appliance receives full voltage and can work independently of the others.

mcqs.q: In which circuit does current have only one path to flow?
mcqs.why: In a series circuit all components are joined one after another in a single loop, giving the current only one path.

mcqs.q: By increasing the number of batteries in a series circuit, the brightness of the bulbs:
mcqs.why: More batteries in series give more voltage, which pushes more current through the bulbs, so they glow brighter.

mcqs.q: Adding more bulbs in a series circuit makes each bulb:
mcqs.why: In series the supply voltage is shared among all the bulbs, so each bulb gets less voltage and glows dimmer as more are added.

mcqs.q: In a parallel circuit, each device receives:
options: The full voltage of the supply
mcqs.why: Every branch of a parallel circuit is connected directly across the supply, so each device gets the full voltage.

mcqs.q: In a parallel circuit, if one bulb fuses:
mcqs.why: Each branch is independent in a parallel circuit, so a fused bulb breaks only its own branch; the others keep glowing.

mcqs.q: A series circuit is not preferred for home wiring because:
options: If one appliance stops, all others also stop working
mcqs.why: With one shared path, a single fused or switched-off appliance breaks the whole circuit, and the voltage is divided among appliances.

mcqs.q: A parallel circuit has:
mcqs.why: The defining feature of a parallel circuit is its two or more branches, each forming its own path for the current.

mcqs.q: In a series circuit, the voltage of the battery is:
mcqs.why: The bulbs in series divide the battery's voltage among themselves, which is why each glows less brightly than a single bulb.

lessons.title: Magnets and Their Poles
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Magnet?

A magnet is a material that attracts magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt — things such as nails, paper clips, scissors and needles. Magnets may be natural (lodestone) or man-made (bar, horseshoe and ring magnets). Every magnet has two ends called poles: a north pole and a south pole.

The Law of Poles

Like poles repel each other (north repels north, south repels south) and unlike poles attract each other. This can be proved by hanging a bar magnet freely and bringing another magnet near it: the suspended magnet moves away from a like pole and is pulled towards an unlike pole.

A Magnet Points North–South

A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest along the north–south direction, its north pole pointing towards the Earth's north. This is why magnets are used in a compass to find directions.

Key Points

  • Magnets attract iron, nickel and cobalt — not wood, plastic or aluminium.
  • The ends of a magnet are called its poles.
  • Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
  • A suspended magnet settles in the north–south direction.

mcqs.q: A magnet can attract objects made of:
mcqs.why: Magnets attract magnetic materials — iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys like steel; wood, plastic and rubber are not attracted.

mcqs.q: The ends of a magnet are called:
mcqs.why: The two ends of a magnet, where its attraction is strongest, are called poles: the north pole and the south pole.

mcqs.q: A freely suspended bar magnet always stays along the:
mcqs.why: The Earth acts like a huge magnet, so a freely suspended magnet aligns itself along the north–south direction.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true?
options: Poles do not affect each other
mcqs.why: Like poles repel: a north pole pushes away another north pole, just as a south pole repels another south pole.

mcqs.q: Unlike poles of two magnets:
mcqs.why: A north pole and a south pole pull towards each other — unlike poles attract, as shown with a suspended magnet experiment.

mcqs.q: A natural magnet found in the earth is called:
mcqs.why: Lodestone is a natural magnetic rock; bar and horseshoe magnets are man-made, and an electromagnet works only with current.

mcqs.q: A compass is used to:
mcqs.why: A compass contains a small magnet (needle) that turns freely and points north–south, helping us find directions.

mcqs.q: When a bar magnet is suspended freely, the end pointing towards the Earth's north is its:
mcqs.why: By definition, the pole of a suspended magnet that settles pointing towards the geographic north is called its north pole.

mcqs.q: Which of these metals is attracted by a magnet?
mcqs.why: Cobalt, like iron and nickel, is a magnetic material attracted by magnets; aluminium, copper and gold are not attracted.

mcqs.q: Which material is NOT attracted by an ordinary magnet?
mcqs.why: Aluminium is a non-magnetic metal: it is not attracted by ordinary magnets and cannot be magnetized in this way.

lessons.title: Magnetic Field and Making Magnets
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic Field

The magnetic field is the space around a magnet in which its force can be felt. It is strongest near the poles and weaker farther away. Field lines are drawn from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. Sprinkling iron filings on paper over a bar magnet shows the field pattern: the filings form curved lines and collect most densely at the poles.

Making a Magnet — Stroking Method

Place an iron or steel bar on a table and stroke it with one pole of a magnet from one end to the other, always in the same direction, lifting the magnet high at the end of each stroke. Repeat 30–40 times. The end where the stroking finishes gets the opposite pole to the stroking pole.

Identifying Poles

To identify the poles of an unmarked magnet, suspend it freely: the end pointing north is the north pole. Repulsion is the sure test of a magnet, because a plain iron bar can attract, but only a magnet can repel a like pole. A plain iron bar hung freely stops in any direction, unlike a magnet.

The Earth's Magnetic Field

The Earth behaves like a huge magnet. Its field is believed to be caused by the movement of molten iron and nickel in its outer core, which produces electric currents that generate the field.

Key Points

  • The magnetic field is strongest at the poles.
  • Iron filings reveal the field pattern of a bar magnet.
  • Stroking must always be in the same direction.
  • Repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.

mcqs.q: The space around a magnet where it can attract magnetic materials is called its:
mcqs.why: The magnetic field is the region around a magnet in which its magnetic force acts on magnetic materials and other magnets.

mcqs.q: The magnetic field of a bar magnet is strongest:
mcqs.why: Field lines are closest together near the poles, showing the field is strongest there and weakens with distance.

mcqs.q: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines are drawn:
options: From south pole to north pole
From north pole to south pole
mcqs.why: By convention, field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet, as iron filings patterns show.

mcqs.q: In the stroking method of making a magnet, the bar is stroked:
options: In both directions turn by turn
mcqs.why: Each stroke must go the same way, lifting the magnet high before returning, so the bar's magnetism builds up in one direction.

mcqs.q: When iron filings are sprinkled over a bar magnet, they collect most densely:
mcqs.why: The filings crowd near the poles because the magnetic field — and hence the attractive force — is strongest at the poles.

mcqs.q: To find the north pole of an unmarked bar magnet, we can:
options: Suspend it freely and see which end points north
mcqs.why: A freely suspended magnet settles north–south; the end pointing towards the Earth's north is its north pole.

mcqs.q: The sure test of a magnet is:
mcqs.why: Both a magnet and an iron bar can attract, but only a magnet repels the like pole of another magnet — so repulsion is the sure test.

mcqs.q: The Earth's magnetic field is believed to be caused by:
options: Movement of molten iron and nickel in the outer core
mcqs.why: Circulating molten iron and nickel in the Earth's outer core produce electric currents, and these currents generate the magnetic field.

mcqs.q: A plain iron bar suspended freely will:
mcqs.why: Only a magnet aligns with the Earth's field; an unmagnetized iron bar has no poles of its own, so it stops in any direction.

mcqs.q: In the stroking method, the end of the bar where stroking finishes gets:
options: The same pole as the stroking pole
The opposite pole to the stroking pole
mcqs.why: Stroking magnetizes the bar so that the finishing end becomes the pole opposite to the pole of the magnet used for stroking.

lessons.title: Electromagnets and Uses of Magnets
lessons.notes_html:
Permanent and Temporary Magnets

A permanent magnet is made of hard material like steel and keeps its magnetism for a long time. A temporary magnet, made of soft iron, acts as a magnet only while near a magnet or while current flows, and loses its magnetism quickly afterwards.

Electromagnets

An electromagnet is a coil of wire wound on an iron core; it becomes a magnet when current flows. Its strength increases with more current, more turns of the coil and a soft iron core — a plastic or wooden core has no such effect. A magnet loses its magnetism if it is heated strongly or hammered/dropped, but not by coating it with oil.

Uses of Magnets and Electromagnets

Magnets are used in compasses, electric bells, loudspeakers, motors, generators, refrigerator doors, scrap-yard cranes and hospital MRI machines. Electromagnets are preferred in bells, motors and cranes because their strength can be controlled and they can be switched on and off. Electricity and magnetism are closely related: a current produces a magnetic field (electromagnet), and a moving magnet produces current (generator).

Key Points

  • Increase current or coil turns to strengthen an electromagnet.
  • An iron core strengthens an electromagnet; plastic does not.
  • Heating or hammering destroys magnetism; oil coating does not.
  • Magnets are not used in a heater.

mcqs.q: A magnet is not used in:
mcqs.why: Compasses, door bells and scrap-yard cranes all use magnets or electromagnets; an electric heater works by a heating element, not a magnet.

mcqs.q: To increase the strength of an electromagnet we should:
options: Insert a wooden core in the coil
Increase the amount of current flowing
mcqs.why: An electromagnet becomes stronger with more current, more turns of coil, or an iron core; a wooden core does nothing.

mcqs.q: Which will NOT cause a magnet to lose its magnetism?
options: Keeping it wrongly near another strong magnet
mcqs.why: Strong heating and hammering disturb a magnet's arrangement and destroy magnetism; a coat of oil only protects the surface.

mcqs.q: Which will NOT increase the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Increasing the number of turns of the coil
mcqs.why: A plastic core is non-magnetic and adds nothing; current, coil turns and a soft iron core all increase an electromagnet's strength.

mcqs.q: Winding more turns of wire on an electromagnet's coil makes it:
mcqs.why: In the paper-clip experiment, the coil with more turns lifts more clips: strength increases with the number of turns.

mcqs.q: Inserting a soft iron core inside the coil of an electromagnet:
mcqs.why: The iron core becomes magnetized and concentrates the field, so the electromagnet can lift much heavier loads than the coil alone.

mcqs.q: Electromagnets are used in scrap-yard cranes because they:
options: Can be switched on to lift iron and off to drop it
mcqs.why: A crane's electromagnet lifts heavy iron when current flows and drops the load when the current is switched off — easy control.

mcqs.q: A permanent magnet is usually made of:
mcqs.why: Steel is a hard magnetic material: once magnetized it keeps its magnetism for a long time, making it suitable for permanent magnets.

mcqs.q: A temporary magnet made of soft iron loses its magnetism:
options: Quickly when the magnet or current is removed
mcqs.why: Soft iron magnetizes easily but also loses its magnetism quickly once the magnet or current is removed — hence 'temporary'.

mcqs.q: Powerful magnets are used in hospitals in:
options: MRI machines to take images of the body
mcqs.why: MRI machines use very powerful magnets to produce detailed images of the inside of the human body for diagnosis.

lessons.title: Growing Vegetables in Season
lessons.notes_html:
Summer and Winter Vegetables

Vegetables are grown in their proper season. Summer season vegetables are sown in February–March and grow in the hot season: brinjal, lady finger (okra), bitter gourd, bottle gourd, pumpkin, cucumber, chillies, tomatoes and mint. Winter season vegetables are sown in September–October and grow in the cool season: turnip, cauliflower, cabbage, carrot, radish, spinach, peas, potato and mustard.

Preparing the Soil Bed

Tools needed for preparing a soil bed for vegetables are: a spade for digging, a hoe/khurpa for loosening the soil and weeding, a rake for levelling, a trowel, a watering can or hose for irrigation, and a measuring tape or rope for marking beds and rows. Manure or fertilizer and seeds or seedlings are also required.

Key Points

  • Summer vegetables: sown February–March (brinjal, lady finger).
  • Winter vegetables: sown September–October (turnip, cauliflower).
  • Spade digs, khurpa loosens and weeds, rake levels the bed.
  • Each vegetable grows best in its own season.

mcqs.q: Summer season vegetables are generally grown (sown) in:
mcqs.why: Summer vegetables like brinjal and lady finger are sown in February–March so that they grow through the hot season.

mcqs.q: Winter season vegetables are grown (sown) in:
mcqs.why: Winter vegetables such as turnip, cauliflower and cabbage are sown in September–October and grow in the cool season.

mcqs.q: Which one is a summer season vegetable?
mcqs.why: Brinjal (eggplant) grows in the hot season and is sown in February–March; turnip, cauliflower and cabbage are winter vegetables.

mcqs.q: Which one is a winter season vegetable?
mcqs.why: Turnip is sown in September–October and grows in the cool season; brinjal, lady finger and bitter gourd are summer vegetables.

mcqs.q: Lady finger (okra) is a:
mcqs.why: Lady finger is listed among the summer season vegetables, sown in February–March along with bitter gourd and cucumber.

mcqs.q: Cauliflower is a:
mcqs.why: Cauliflower grows well in the cool season and is sown in September–October, like cabbage, carrot and spinach.

mcqs.q: The tool used for digging the soil bed is the:
mcqs.why: A spade is the digging tool; a rake levels the bed, a watering can irrigates, and a tape only marks out the beds and rows.

mcqs.q: The tool used for levelling the prepared soil bed is the:
mcqs.why: After digging and loosening, a rake is drawn over the bed to level the surface evenly for sowing seeds.

mcqs.q: A hoe (khurpa) is used for:
mcqs.why: The khurpa (hoe) loosens the soil around plants and removes weeds, helping air and water reach the roots.

mcqs.q: Winter season vegetables grow well in:
mcqs.why: Winter vegetables are adapted to cool weather; they are sown in September–October and harvested during the winter months.

lessons.title: Fertilizers and Pesticides
lessons.notes_html:
Fertilizers

Fertilizers are substances added to the soil to provide essential nutrients which plants need for growth and which the soil loses after repeated crops. Chemical fertilizers mainly provide the elements nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K): urea gives nitrogen, DAP gives nitrogen and phosphorus, and potash gives potassium. Natural (organic) fertilizers include farmyard manure and compost. Fertilizers increase crop yield, but excessive use can damage the soil and pollute water.

Pesticides

Pesticides are chemical substances used to kill or control pests — insects, weeds and fungi — that damage crops. They protect crops from heavy losses, increase food production, protect stored grains, and protect public health, for example sprays against mosquitoes that spread dengue and malaria. They must be used in the correct dose, because excess harms helpful insects, soil, water and human health.

Key Points

  • Fertilizers provide plants with nutrients, not water or sunlight.
  • Urea = nitrogen; DAP = nitrogen + phosphorus; potash = potassium.
  • Manure and compost are natural fertilizers.
  • Pesticides control crop pests but must be used carefully.

mcqs.q: Fertilizers provide plants with:
mcqs.why: Fertilizers supply the essential nutrient elements — mainly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — that plants take from the soil.

mcqs.q: Chemical fertilizers mainly provide the elements:
mcqs.why: The three main elements supplied by chemical fertilizers are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K).

mcqs.q: Urea is a fertilizer that provides plants with:
mcqs.why: Urea is a nitrogen fertilizer; it promotes green, leafy growth of crops. DAP gives nitrogen and phosphorus, potash gives potassium.

mcqs.q: DAP fertilizer provides:
mcqs.why: DAP (diammonium phosphate) supplies two nutrients together: nitrogen and phosphorus, both needed for healthy crop growth.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a natural (organic) fertilizer?
mcqs.why: Farmyard manure and compost are natural fertilizers made from animal and plant waste; urea, DAP and potash are chemical fertilizers.

mcqs.q: Excessive use of chemical fertilizers can:
options: Damage the soil and pollute water
Kill all germs in the air
mcqs.why: Too much fertilizer harms soil life and washes into water, polluting it; fertilizers should be used in the right amount only.

mcqs.q: Pesticides are used to:
options: Kill or control pests that damage crops
mcqs.why: Pesticides are chemicals that kill or control insects, weeds and fungi which attack crops and reduce the harvest.

mcqs.q: Pesticides also protect:
mcqs.why: Besides crops, pesticides protect stored grains from insects and kill disease-carrying mosquitoes, protecting public health.

mcqs.q: Sprays against mosquitoes help to prevent:
mcqs.why: Mosquitoes spread dengue and malaria, so controlling them with sprays is an important use of pesticides for public health.

mcqs.q: Potash fertilizer provides plants with the element:
mcqs.why: Potash is the potassium fertilizer; together nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the three main fertilizer elements.

lessons.title: Technology in Food and Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Making Yogurt and Cheese

For yogurt (dahi) we need fresh milk and a little previous yogurt as a starter culture of helpful bacteria; the boiled milk is cooled to lukewarm, mixed with the starter and kept warm until it sets. (Red chilly is not used!) For cheese (paneer) at home we need milk, lemon juice (or vinegar) to curdle it, and a little salt; the curdled solid is separated through muslin cloth and pressed. Sugar is not used in cheese.

Microorganisms in the Food Industry

Helpful microbes do useful work: bacteria (Lactobacillus) turn milk into yogurt and cheese, and yeast makes bread rise and is used in other fermented foods, pickles and vinegar.

Technology Around Us

An electric bell works on the principle of an electromagnet: current makes the coil attract an iron strip whose hammer strikes the gong, breaking and remaking the circuit rapidly. A solar oven cooks food with trapped sunlight, saving fuel without pollution. Technology serves us in homes, communication, transport, health, agriculture and education, but careless use — excess screens, pollution, too many chemicals — can be harmful.

Key Points

  • Yogurt needs milk and a starter culture — not red chilly.
  • Cheese is made by curdling milk with lemon juice.
  • Yeast makes bread rise; Lactobacillus makes yogurt.
  • An electric bell works with an electromagnet.

mcqs.q: Which is not used in the preparation of yogurt?
mcqs.why: Yogurt is made from milk with a starter culture, using a spoon and thermometer; red chilly plays no part in making yogurt.

mcqs.q: Which is not used in making cheese at home?
mcqs.why: Cheese (paneer) needs milk, lemon juice to curdle it and a little salt; sugar is not used in making cheese.

mcqs.q: Yogurt sets because of the action of:
options: Helpful bacteria in the starter culture
mcqs.why: The starter yogurt contains Lactobacillus bacteria, which multiply in warm milk and turn it into set yogurt.

mcqs.q: In making cheese at home, milk is curdled by adding:
mcqs.why: Lemon juice (or vinegar) is the curdling agent: it separates the milk into solid curd and liquid whey, and the curd is pressed into cheese.

mcqs.q: An electric bell works on the principle of:
mcqs.why: When current flows, the bell's coil becomes an electromagnet, pulls the iron strip, and the hammer strikes the gong again and again.

mcqs.q: A solar oven cooks food using:
mcqs.why: A solar oven traps and concentrates sunlight inside a black box with a glass lid, heating the food without any fuel or pollution.

mcqs.q: The microorganism used to make bread rise is:
mcqs.why: Yeast is a fungus that ferments the dough and produces gas, making the bread rise and become soft and spongy.

mcqs.q: The bacteria that turn milk into yogurt are:
mcqs.why: Lactobacillus bacteria in the starter culture convert milk into yogurt and are also used in making cheese.

mcqs.q: Excessive use of mobile phones and screens can harm:
mcqs.why: Among the harmful effects of technology, too much screen time damages the eyes and health — technology must be used wisely.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the use of technology in agriculture?
mcqs.why: Modern agriculture uses technology — tractors for ploughing, fertilizers for nutrients and tube wells for irrigation — to raise production.

lessons.title: The Sun, Planets and Heavenly Bodies
lessons.notes_html:
Stars and Planets

Stars are huge heavenly bodies that emit their own light and heat; the Sun is a star and the only body in our list that emits its own light. Planets do not emit light; they shine by reflecting sunlight and revolve around the Sun in fixed orbits. There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars (inner, rocky) and Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune (outer, giant gaseous). Jupiter is the largest planet and Mercury is the nearest to the Sun; Venus orbits inside (before) the orbit of Earth.

Dwarf Planets, Asteroids and Comets

Dwarf planets like Pluto are round but have not cleared their orbits. Asteroids are small rocky objects revolving around the Sun, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are bodies of ice, dust and rock; near the Sun they grow a glowing head and a long tail that always points away from the Sun. Halley's comet returns after about every 76 years.

Meteors and Meteorites

A meteor is a rocky object burning up in the atmosphere, seen as a bright streak (a shooting star). A meteorite is the part that survives and lands on the Earth's surface.

Key Points

  • The Sun is a star; planets shine by reflected light.
  • Jupiter is the largest planet; Mercury is nearest the Sun.
  • A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
  • A meteor burns in the sky; a meteorite lands on the ground.

mcqs.q: The largest planet of our solar system is:
mcqs.why: Jupiter is the giant of the solar system — the largest planet, bigger than all the other planets' masses combined.

mcqs.q: The nearest planet to the Sun is:
mcqs.why: Mercury is the innermost planet, orbiting closest to the Sun; Venus comes next, then Earth and Mars.

mcqs.q: Which one emits its own light?
mcqs.why: The Sun is a star and produces its own light and heat; the Moon, Earth and Venus only reflect the Sun's light.

mcqs.q: Venus orbits before (inside the orbit of):
mcqs.why: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth — so Venus's orbit lies inside Earth's orbit, closer to the Sun.

mcqs.q: The tail of a comet points:
mcqs.why: The solar wind pushes the comet's gases away, so its tail always streams away from the Sun, whichever way the comet moves.

mcqs.q: The total number of planets in our solar system is:
mcqs.why: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; Pluto is now classed as a dwarf planet.

mcqs.q: Pluto is now classified as a:
mcqs.why: Pluto is a dwarf planet: it is round and orbits the Sun, but it has not cleared its orbit of other objects like the true planets.

mcqs.q: Most asteroids are found:
mcqs.why: Most asteroids revolve in the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, leftovers from the solar system's formation.

mcqs.q: A bright streak of light in the sky, called a shooting star, is a:
mcqs.why: A meteor is a small rocky object burning up by friction in the atmosphere, appearing as a brief bright streak — a shooting star.

mcqs.q: Halley's comet appears after about every:
mcqs.why: Halley's comet has a long elliptical orbit and becomes visible from Earth after about every 76 years.

lessons.title: Satellites and Space Technology
lessons.notes_html:
Natural and Artificial Satellites

A natural satellite revolves around a planet by nature — the Moon is Earth's natural satellite. Artificial satellites are man-made objects launched into space for communication, weather forecasting, navigation and research; Pakistan's PakSat-1R is one example. The first artificial satellite was sent into space in 1957. A geostationary satellite completes one orbit around the Earth in one day, so it stays over the same place.

GPS

The GPS (Global Positioning System) locates the position of an object on the Earth's surface. Satellites continuously send signals with their position and the exact time; a receiver compares signals from at least four satellites and calculates its own exact position, shown on a map.

Exploring Space

Astronomers predict eclipses, comet appearances and planet positions. Space telescopes like Hubble take clear pictures without the disturbance of the atmosphere. Mars is the planet man is most likely to travel to: it is near, has a day of about 24.6 hours, seasons, a solid surface and water ice at its poles.

Key Points

  • The Moon is a natural satellite; PakSat-1R is artificial.
  • The first artificial satellite was launched in 1957.
  • A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth in one day.
  • GPS needs signals from at least four satellites.

mcqs.q: A geostationary satellite completes one orbit around the Earth in:
mcqs.why: A geostationary satellite takes one day (24 hours) per orbit, matching the Earth's rotation, so it appears fixed over one place.

mcqs.q: The system that locates the position of an object on the surface of Earth is:
mcqs.why: GPS — the Global Positioning System — uses satellite signals to fix the exact position of a receiver anywhere on Earth.

mcqs.q: The first artificial satellite was sent into space in:
mcqs.why: The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957; the first Moon landing came later, in 1969.

mcqs.q: The natural satellite of the Earth is:
mcqs.why: The Moon revolves around the Earth naturally, so it is Earth's natural satellite; the others are man-made or independent bodies.

mcqs.q: PakSat-1R is an example of:
mcqs.why: PakSat-1R is a man-made communication satellite launched by Pakistan, so it is an artificial satellite of the Earth.

mcqs.q: A GPS receiver needs signals from at least ________ satellites to fix its position.
mcqs.why: By comparing the arrival times of signals from at least four satellites, the receiver calculates its distance from each and fixes its position.

mcqs.q: The planet man is most likely to travel to is:
mcqs.why: Mars is near, has a solid surface, a day of about 24.6 hours, seasons and water ice — the most Earth-like target for human travel.

mcqs.q: The length of a day on Mars is about:
mcqs.why: Mars rotates in about 24.6 hours, very close to Earth's day, one of the reasons it is the most likely planet for human missions.

mcqs.q: Astronomers make predictions about:
options: Eclipses and the appearance of comets
mcqs.why: From the regular movements of heavenly bodies, astronomers predict solar and lunar eclipses, comet appearances and planet positions.

mcqs.q: Space telescopes like Hubble take clear pictures because they work:
options: Above the disturbance of the atmosphere
mcqs.why: Orbiting above the atmosphere, space telescopes avoid its blurring and take sharp pictures of stars, galaxies and planets.

lessons.title: Staying Safe from Corona Virus
lessons.notes_html:
Precautions for Going to the Market

The book's appendix activity lists the precautionary measures to follow during the corona virus outbreak when going out, for example to the market:

  • Wear a mask before going out.
  • Do not go to the market daily; go only when needed and avoid crowded times.
  • Keep a sanitizer and use it regularly, and avoid touching the face.
  • Do not go to the market if you have a cough or fever.
  • After returning, do not touch the purchased items for a few hours, and wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly before use.
  • People above 60 years of age and children under 15 should especially avoid going to crowded markets.

Key Points

  • Mask, sanitizer and avoiding crowds are the basic precautions.
  • A person with cough or fever should stay home.
  • Wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly after bringing them home.

mcqs.q: Before going to the market during the corona outbreak, a person should:
mcqs.why: The book's guidelines say to wear a mask before going out, as the first precaution against the corona virus in public places.

mcqs.q: Sanitizer should be used:
options: Regularly, while avoiding touching the face
mcqs.why: The guidelines advise keeping a sanitizer, using it regularly during the outing, and avoiding touching the face with unwashed hands.

mcqs.q: Visits to the market should be:
options: Made only when needed, avoiding crowded times
mcqs.why: Going only when needed and avoiding crowded times reduces contact with other people and lowers the risk of infection.

mcqs.q: A person who has a cough or fever should:
mcqs.why: The guidelines clearly state: do not go to the market if you have a cough or fever, to protect yourself and others.

mcqs.q: After returning from the market, fruits and vegetables should be:
mcqs.why: Purchased fruits and vegetables must be washed thoroughly before use, and the items should not be touched for a few hours after returning.

mcqs.q: After returning home, the purchased items should:
options: Not be touched for a few hours
mcqs.why: The guidelines advise leaving the purchased items untouched for a few hours after returning, as a precaution against the virus.

mcqs.q: People who should especially avoid crowded markets are those:
mcqs.why: Older people above 60 are at greater risk from the corona virus, so they should especially avoid going to crowded markets.

mcqs.q: Children of which age should especially avoid crowded markets?
mcqs.why: The guidelines say children under 15 years, like people above 60, should especially avoid crowded markets during the outbreak.

mcqs.q: The purpose of using a sanitizer is to:
mcqs.why: A sanitizer kills germs picked up from surfaces and money during shopping, reducing the chance of infection through the hands.

mcqs.q: All these precautions are taken to protect us from:
mcqs.why: This appendix activity of the book lists safety measures specifically for the corona virus outbreak when going out to public places.
